Translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Liang Dynasty,
from the "Chapter on the Ground of the Mind," Part Two:
Briefly explaining that the self-cause, as comprised within the conditions for arising, is fully present— this is termed "arrival."
What constitutes "attainment" (*prāpti*)?
Because the causes appear abbreviated, the causal conditions are fully present, and thus [the effect] arises; therefore, it is called "attainment.

Through such discernment, one knows that it exists as a conventional designation (*prajñapti*). If it were substantially existent (*dravyasat*), there would be two kinds: namely, existence as a productive cause (*janakahetu*) and existence as an inseparable cause (*avinirbhāgahetu*).
If there were a cause for arising, then since the time when a dharma has not yet been attained, how could it arise by having non-existence as its cause?
If this were the case, it would never arise at all.
Since it exists apart from the causes of dharmas, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas would all arise simultaneously; furthermore, obstructive dharmas should likewise arise together.
Therefore, both types of causes are untenable.

Furthermore, the cause that gives rise to phenomena is the cause consisting of its own seeds, which are encompassed by their respective manifest conditions; because it is precisely these seeds, they are called "arrival" (*prāpti*).
Because other distinct causes and conditions are present before one, it is called "separation from other conditions."
In this context, it is by means of this sovereignty that it is conventionally designated as "arrival.

This sovereignty refers to those persons for whom all phenomena are produced and ceased; because further craving manifests and swiftly draws forth the conditions for birth, it is therefore called "arrival."
Briefly, there are three meanings:
first, the accomplishment of the seeds;
second, the accomplishment of mastery.
Third is the accomplishment of manifestation.

Regarding the accomplishment of seeds: all unwholesome dharmas, various indeterminate dharmas, and innate wholesome dharmas that arise without effort—these seeds have not yet been definitively destroyed by the Noble Path and severed;
nor have the various wholesome seeds been destroyed by false views. This is called the accomplishment of seeds.
How is this known?
As long as the seeds of all phenomena have not yet been destroyed, whether unwholesome phenomena are manifest or unmanifest, such persons are all said to be "accomplished" [in them].

That which is produced by the power of various wholesome dharmas, wherein all causes subsumed under the conditions for the arising of the indeterminate are fully present, is called "attainment through mastery.
That various present dharmas arise because they exist before one's eyes as their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) is called "attainment through presence."
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
Based on past karma, one receives a body in various places; being drawn by karma, one dwells for a limited duration. That which draws forth this life is precisely what is called the life-faculty.

Furthermore, the analysis of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is twofold: namely, determinate and indeterminate; following [the body] and not following it; limited and extensive; having an end and being without end; and possessing mastery and lacking mastery.
The lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa, once departed from its full extent, has a fixed remainder; within Jambudvīpa,
lifespans may be immeasurable or brief, even down to ten years,
whereas the people of Uttarakuru have a fixed lifespan of one thousand years.
In this place, death occurs according to the span of life without further conditions; in other places, it does not.
Among the people of Jambudvīpa whose lifespan is ten years, this is called short-lived;
there are certain animals that die and are reborn seven times within a single day, and even within a single day and night.
The lifespan of the gods in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is eighty thousand great kalpas; the lifespan of Arhats likewise has a subsequent existence.

If those who are still in training (śaikṣas) enter nirvāṇa in the present life, and for ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) their final birth-body has a subsequent existence, then for all other persons there is no further subsequent existence.
The Arhats, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas possess mastery over the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and are able to prolong their lifespan; others do not attain such mastery over their lifespan.
What is meant by "the various categories of sentient beings"?

Briefly stated, regarding the various classes of sentient beings who take birth in various places—those who share the same realm, the same path, the same birth, the same species, the same age, and the same surname, as well as those with similar conduct such as height and so forth—it is by depending on these divisions that they are all similar; this is called the "similarity of the class of sentient beings."

There are sentient beings who, based on these categories of realms (*dhātu*), each possess corresponding portions; within a single realm, sentient beings undergo birth because they each possess corresponding portions according to the five destinies (*gati*).

Within each destiny, there are sentient beings who undergo birth based on their divisions of birth; within each successive birth, they are born according to their categories and their respective lineages.
There are sentient beings whose physical forms, voices, and activities appear similar; there are sentient beings whose virtues and evils appear similar, each having their own semblances.
For example, those who kill live together with other killers, and so on, up to those with wrong views living together with others who hold wrong views;
likewise, those who abstain from killing live together with others who abstain from killing, and so on, up to those with right views living together with others who hold right views.

A stream-enterer together with a stream-enterer, up to a pratyekabuddha with a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva with a bodhisattva, and a buddha with a buddha—this is called the "category of similarity."
All sentient beings are merely provisional designations; how could sentient beings be real dharmas even if they appear to have distinct divisions?

As for the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*): it is the state in which the seeds of the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering within the three realms have not yet been severed; this is called the nature of an ordinary person.
Furthermore, there are four types of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*):

first, those lacking the nature for *nirvāṇa*; second, those subsumed under the nature of a *śrāvaka*; [third, those subsumed under the nature of a *pratyekabuddha*; and fourth, those subsumed under the nature of a *tathāgata*].
Third, it is subsumed within the nature of the pratyekabuddha;
fourth, it is subsumed within the Buddha-nature.
Apart from the ten afflictions, there is no distinct nature that can be called the "nature of an ordinary person" (pṛthagjanatva).
What is the nature of conjunction?
When causes and conditions are fully assembled, all phenomena arise.
That various phenomena arise from various causes and conditions is called the "cooperative cause" (*sahakāri-hetu*).
As for the nature of conjunction, there are further six kinds:
conjunction of sensation;
conjunction of the arising of the sense bases; and so forth.
Sixth, the harmony of entering and abiding;
the harmony of skillful knowledge;
and the harmony of purity.
They arise in mutual conjunction.

As for the experience of this conjunction: consciousnesses arise based on the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) and mental attention (*manasikāra*). Through the conjunction of these three factors, contact (*sparśa*) arises; and through the conjunction of contact, feeling (*vedanā*) arises.
The conjunction of arising consists of ignorance as the condition for volitional formations, up to old age and death.
The conjunction of abiding consists of reliance upon the four nutriments and the life-faculty.
The conjunction of craftsmanship consists of the skillful knowledge, the tools, and human effort; this is called the conjunction of craftsmanship.
As for the conjunction of purity, it refers to the twelve difficult-to-attain powers of oneself and others.

Regarding those who are harmoniously united through mutual association: it is as if there were a person who, as the ruler of a great kingdom, governs and transforms according to the Dharma; sentient beings rely upon him, and the four seas enjoy peace and tranquility.
Apart from such constituent parts, there is no separate "harmony."

Regarding the combination of syllables (*vyañjana*): they are established as provisional designations based on the characteristics of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Based on such meanings, these are called syllables. Regarding the combination of phrases (*pada*):

having already explained [the categories of] phenomena according to their own characteristics—wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, pure and impure phenomena—one selects and discriminates among them, uniting names to form phrases; this is the combination of phrases.
The "combination of flavor" (*vyañjana-saṃnipāta*) refers to the conjunction of names and phrases, wherein the meaning of the syllables is fully complete; this is the combination of flavor.

Among all concise meanings, these are entirely "names" (*nāman*); regarding meanings of intermediate length, they are called "phrases" (*pada*); and regarding meanings that are extensively explained, they are termed "flavor" (*vyañjana*).
Relying solely on names, one knows only names and does not know their meaning.
If one relies on phrases, one knows the nature of all phenomena and also knows the sounds [of those names], yet one cannot extensively discern the various phenomena.
Based on the collection of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), one understands the meaning of all phenomena.

By means of these collections of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), one understands conventional designations within the five fields of training; these names are established differently according to regional vernaculars.
If there were no difference in location within the resonance, it would be heard by the ear because of its auditory nature.
What are the five bases of training?
The first is internal training;
Second, the study of causes;
third, the study of sounds;
fourth, the study of medical arts.
Fifth is the mundane study of arts and crafts.
What is arising?
The uninterrupted continuity of the causes and effects of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is called arising.
Furthermore, there is the arising of birth through the seed of existence, just as all phenomena arise from their seeds.
Moreover, there is the arising of birth through the fruit of the seed of existence, such as when the original seed has not yet been extinguished and the manifestation of that seed arises.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, there is birth from the stream of names; among the four non-material aggregates (*arūpaskandha*), there is birth from the stream of matter (*rūpadhātu*).

This is like the ten internal and external bases (*āyatana*); within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), there is the arising of unmanifest matter (*avijñaptirūpa*), and there is birth following the stream.

Just as there are twelve links of dependent origination in direct order, there are also twelve links of dependent origination in reverse order; it is by means of these that birth arises, which is simply a continuous succession and not a separate entity.
What is the principle of fixed limits?

It is because, based on the seeds of individual fixed limits from beginningless time, the phenomena of cause and effect do not intermingle; for whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, the nature of phenomena remains eternally as it is.
There is a limit of cessation, such as the twelve links of dependent origination in their direct and reverse orders.
There is a limit of the True Dharma, meaning that the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth, neither increase nor decrease.
There is the limit of experience (*vedanā-pariccheda*), such as the three types of feeling (*trivedanā-dharma*), which likewise neither increase nor decrease.
There is the limit of abiding (*sthiti-pariccheda*), meaning that all bodies, up to and including life-span and all external phenomena, abide for one great eon (*mahākalpa*).
There is a limit to transformation: for example, when sentient beings who have already been born in the form realm fall back and are born in the desire realm, there is a definite limit;
likewise, when sentient beings are born in places possessing form, their bodies have a definite limit, and the external world of dharmas also has a definite limit.
What is meant by "that which is appropriate"?

It refers to the teaching of all dharmas, the establishing of all dharmas, and the correct knowledge of dharmas; herein, the skillful means is termed "the appropriate. There are four distinctions: first, the appropriate through vision; [second, the appropriate through hearing; third, the appropriate through practice;
fourth, the appropriate through realization].
Second is the appropriate response to a question;
third is the appropriate response regarding the meaning of a treatise;
fourth is the appropriate response based on the nature of things (*dharmatā*), as will be explained in detail later in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
What is swift? All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise and perish so swiftly that they do not remain; the swiftness of conditioned activity is precisely this arising and perishing.
There is also the swiftness of power and force, namely terrestrial movement, such as that of elephants, horses, and humans.
Furthermore, there are swift movements such as those of the *khecaras*, celestial birds, and various *yakṣas*,
which are as rapid as the moment a sound is emitted;
and there are swift movements of water, such as the flow of rivers.
The swiftness of fire is like a great, fierce flame consuming dry grass.
The swiftness of archery is like a skilled archer whose arrows travel with rapidity.
The swiftness of wisdom refers to the various noble ones who, through discernment and cultivation, swiftly comprehend all meanings.
"Swift in movement" refers to the great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), whereby the body is transported with extreme speed.
"Swift in mind" refers to the swiftness of the mind and the rapidity of supernormal power.
What is succession?
When various formations arise in a continuous stream, each succeeding one following its predecessor in order, this is called succession.
There is also a succession of arising, such as that of the twelve links of dependent origination.

There is a sequence of cessation, following the reverse order of dependent origination: because ignorance ceases, everything up to old age and death ceases; because old age and death cease, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction all cease.

Furthermore, there is the sequential order for the practices of both monastics and laypeople: rising at dawn to attend to the body, donning clothes and attending to affairs, engaging in play and testing one's skills, bathing, anointing with fragrant oils, adorning the body with flowers, partaking of various foods and drinks, and resting or sleeping—this is the sequence for the laity.
What is the sequence of the path-dharma? It is as follows:

rising at dawn in the same sequence as before, up to putting on one's robes, taking up the alms-bowl, and begging for food; having obtained food, returning and sitting down to eat; washing the hands, wiping the bowl, cleansing the feet, and sitting in meditation; preaching, reciting, and engaging in wholesome reflection; and during the day, practicing walking, standing, and sitting—these two types of activities serve to remedy mental hindrances and are the methods for cultivation.
At midnight, one should lie down to rest; during the latter part of the night, one should rise quickly to perform such tasks as putting on robes.

Within the great assembly, according to seniority, one should respectfully inquire after others' well-being and sit in the proper order, distributing voting sticks (*śalākā*) and receiving bedding in accordance with the Dharma.
There is the sequence of birth, which consists of eight stages from childhood to old age.
Furthermore, there is the sequence of seeing the truths (satya), wherein one first contemplates the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya), followed by the truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
Furthermore, there is the sequence of the nine meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihāra*).

Furthermore, there is the sequence of training (*śikṣā*): by relying on the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*), one gives rise to the training in concentration (*citta-śikṣā*), and subsequently gives rise to the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
What is meant by "time"?
Based on the rising and setting of the sun, one discerns the limits of temporal divisions.
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) possess arising and ceasing, the designations of the three periods of time are established; thus, "time" is designated by means of these names.
This includes such phenomena as years and seasons, months and fortnights, days and nights, *kṣaṇas*, *lava-s*, and *muhūrta-s*, as well as the past, present, and future.
Regarding what is called "time" (*kāla*): apart from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dharma*), there is no separate time.
What is called "number" (*saṃkhyā*)?
It is the enumeration of various distinct phenomena to make known their quantity; this is what is meant by number.

Furthermore, regarding enumeration: starting from one or two dharmas up to many numbers, and continuing beyond those numbers, it is called *asaṃkhyeya* (incalculable), because beyond this point there are no further names for numbers.
What is the seed?

Apart from the dharmas of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), there is no separate seed; because these formations arise in such a way and proceed in such a way, they are called the "seed," and they are also called the "fruit."
The effect and the cause are distinct and must not be viewed as conflated.
Why are they not conflated?

One knows the past cause by means of the present effect, and one knows the future effect by means of the present cause; since this cause is also termed an "effect," cause and effect are not conflated.
Just as with grains such as rice and barley, from the sprout, leaf, stalk, and node—whether unopened or already opened—there is no separate seed apart from these phenomena.
Observing in this way, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) possess the characteristic of being a seed.
It has already been explained how the seeds of unwholesome dharmas are severed and destroyed.
What, then, severs and destroys the seeds of wholesome dharmas?
First, by constantly engaging in unwholesome dharmas, which are contrary to the wholesome, one severs and destroys the roots of goodness.
Second, because they are attached to wrong views and because those wrong views are grave, they also sever their roots of goodness, as do the various non-Buddhists.
Third, because of their wrong views, they slander all [teachings] and commit the five heinous crimes, thereby also severing their roots of goodness.

Fourth, when the seeds of unwholesome and evil dharmas have already been severed, the roots of goodness are likewise severed, as is the case with an Anāgāmin or a Bodhisattva who has attained the stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the seeds of all dharmas form a single aggregate; having completed the giving of their fruit, they reach the fruit itself, categorized as weak, medium, or superior.
Furthermore, to speak briefly of the characteristics of the various seeds that reside within the ālayavijñāna:

all dharmas are attached to the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of false conceptualization (*parikalpita*). By virtue of these habit-energies, they are called both "substantial dharmas" and "provisional names. From these dharmas there is no separate characteristic, yet there is no characteristic that is not separate from them, just like the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).

Furthermore, if habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) pervade all places and encompass the seeds of all phenomena (*dharma*) based upon these various evil and sinful dharmas, then what serves as the basis for the arising of supramundane dharmas?
The seeds of all unwholesome dharmas do not serve as their cause; rather, these supramundane dharmas arise by taking the realm of *tathatā* (suchness) as their condition.
If they were to arise without taking habituation as a condition, for what reason would you proclaim the three natures of *nirvāṇa*?
Furthermore, it is said that some individuals lack the nature for *nirvāṇa*.

This is indeed the case: all sentient beings possess the realm of *tathatā*, yet because they encounter conditions that either obstruct or do not obstruct [the realization of] it, their liberation varies accordingly.

There are sentient beings who possess seeds that are eternally obstructed and are unable to penetrate the realm of *tathatā* (suchness); for these sentient beings, it is said that they lack the nature of *nirvāṇa*.

There are other sentient beings who do not rely on this principle when speaking of the nature of *nirvāṇa*; their various cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are eternally based upon the fundamental [seeds], yet these are not the seeds of obstruction for liberation. Clarifying this principle, there exists the nature of a *śrāvaka* and the nature of a *pratyekabuddha*.
This is not like the previous principle; it is called the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and therefore there is no fault.
The continuity produced by the supramundane dharmas abides by relying upon the amala-vijñāna.

This continuity serves as the antidote to the ālaya-vijñāna; being itself without a place of abiding, it is the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu), free from the toil of evil and devoid of all afflictions.
What constitutes "conditioned activity"?
Briefly stated, there are three types:
first, impure phenomena;
The second is wholesome dharmas;
the third is indeterminate dharmas.

Regarding "impure action," this refers to the ten unwholesome paths of karma. When these arise from body, speech, and mind and are practiced without cessation, they serve as the predominant condition. This bodily and vocal karma causes others to take cognizance of it; this is called "impurity."

One who performs wholesome dharmas refrains from these ten unwholesome actions and does not practice them; when this bodily and vocal karma causes others to know [one's virtue], it is called "wholesome performance.
As for the indeterminate, such as these modes of deportment or various crafts, this bodily and vocal karma is an indeterminate performance.

Furthermore, there are various karmas that do not cause others to know them, but are initiated solely by one's own mind; because one perceives speech within this mind based on dharmas such as wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, these are called "mental actions."
Only that which arises from the body as this non-different phenomenon is called bodily action (kāyakarman);
it is not physical movement.
Why? Because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) perish moment by moment, they have no destination to reach.
That which consists solely of speech is called verbal action (*vākkarma*).
Such mental activity and this process of reflection are what constitute mental action (*manaskarma*). Why is this so?
Because things perish in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), it is not logical that they move from here to there.

Apart from the arising of formations (*saṃskāra*), there is no other karma; nor can the eyes, ears, mind, and so forth perceive [such movement]. Therefore, the "agent" (*kartṛ*) also exists only as a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
If there are people who follow evil associates and are born in that place, they gradually grow up and reflect to themselves:
"It is by means of these activities that I have obtained this life; thus, I shall joyfully practice patience through such karmic conduct."
At that time, it is known that he lacks protection; because of his unwholesome roots, he has no protection whatsoever.
Since he is gripped by the power of intense and profound improper reflection, this person immediately acquires great unwholesome roots.

This person has not yet acquired the unwholesome [karma] of killing, nor have they realized the other unwholesome courses of action; as long as they have not yet performed them, there is no transgression. However, from the moment they perform them, unwholesomeness arises again in accordance with the time and the specific karma involved.
It is just as when people in a former life dwell among evil friends; each, according to their kind, increases their evil karma in the same way. Thus it is:

as long as one does not abandon thoughts that lack protection, there will be no protection. Because such thoughts increase day by day and because such karma is performed, all unwholesome roots come to grow.

Because it functions in conjunction with unwholesome thoughts, lack of faith, indolence, forgetfulness, distracted clinging, and faulty wisdom, it causes one to habituate to these karmas and perform these karmas; thus, from this point onward, there exists the seed and the root.
Because it has been practiced habitually, that which is present within the continuum is called "unprotected.

Based on the causes of relinquishment, as long as one has not yet abandoned the lack of faith in knowledge, herein the commission of evil karma and the lack of belief that there are evil retributions in future lives is termed "lack of faith" (*āśraddhya*).
As for indolence (*kausīdya*): to dwell at will within these unwholesome states and be unable to abandon them is called indolence.
As for forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*): when there are various faults that are censured by the wise, failing to manifest them as they truly are is called forgetfulness.
As for "clinging" (*ālambana*), the mind is afflicted and distracted; this mental continuum arises constantly without abiding, which is called "cramping clinging.
As for "evil wisdom" (*duṣprajñā*), by means of this inversion one regards evil as good and good as evil; this is called "evil wisdom."

With the observance of unwholesome precepts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), these unwholesome factors and other such unwholesome phenomena arise, accompanied by evil volition (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).

When one does not abide in these unwholesome precepts and does not rely on the former [conditions], according to the principle of reality (*yathābhūta-yukti*), this is termed wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*).

Distinguishing them in this way, if there are persons capable of receiving the precepts, they are granted the wholesome precepts; just as some persons receive the precepts from others, they may also receive them from themselves, such that there are those who obtain the self-precepts without receiving them from another.
Only the bhikṣu precepts. Why?
Because none of the bhikṣu precepts can be received by all people.

If a bhikṣu’s precepts were not received from another—whether one was capable of receiving them or incapable—and if everyone could personally attain the precepts of renunciation on their own, then the Dharma and Vinaya established by the Tathāgata would not endure.
The formal exposition of the legal precepts is difficult to understand; therefore, the monastic code of a bhikṣu cannot be acquired through self-ordination.
If it were possible to acquire various precepts independently of the bhikṣu code, why would one receive these precepts from another?
The guarding of the precepts has two aspects:
self-shame and shame before others.
When one wishes to transgress the precepts, one feels shame before others; it is in this way that the precepts are obtained from others.
Regarding "self-shame": when one personally guards and maintains [the precepts] without any transgression, this is called attaining the precepts.

Where there is self-shame, there is also shame regarding others; however, where there is shame regarding others, it does not necessarily entail self-shame. Therefore, self-shame is more powerful in terms of the power of the Dharma.
If one receives [the precepts] for oneself and maintains them well, the merit produced is without distinction; however, if one receives them from another, such differences arise.

One should first resolve to generate the mind [of awakening], personally visit and request a teacher, perform acts of prostration and other services according to the Dharma, and contemplate the words spoken so that the teacher understands what is being done; this is called the preliminary preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*) of the actions of body, speech, and mind.
If one attains it through personal realization, it is produced solely by the mind.

For those who are detached from volition (*cetanā*), this is not protection; however, when the five faculties such as faith take detachment from volition as their dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), it is called protection.

Furthermore, there are one hundred aspects to the upholding of the precepts. These arise from the undertaking of abstention based on the ten unwholesome paths of action; for instance, within the precept against killing, one may undertake only a single portion, and so on, up to holding only a fragmentary portion of the precept against wrong view—these are called the ten types.
In the precept against killing, one may receive it in many parts, up to and including wrong view; these constitute ten distinct types.
Furthermore, there are another ten distinct types, ranging from the complete observance of the precept against taking life up to wrong view.

These further comprise ten types: if one observes the precepts from abstaining from killing up to abstaining from wrong views for a short duration—whether for a single day and night, a half-month, or even up to a year—these are called the ten types.
If one receives the precepts from non-killing up to wrong view for a period exceeding many lifetimes but does not reach the end of that lifespan, there are another ten types.
Furthermore, if one receives the precepts from non-killing up to wrong view until the very end of one's lifespan, there are yet another ten distinct types.
Having undertaken the precepts against killing, not killing living beings upon seeing them, and so on up to wrong views—these are called the ten kinds.
Having personally undertaken these wholesome precepts and further encouraging others to undertake them—these constitute another ten kinds.
Praising the precepts with virtuous speech consists of ten further types.
Having received [the vows] from non-killing up to wrong view, one spontaneously gives rise to joy; these are called the ten types.
These ten types of characteristics for receiving the precepts combine to form one hundred; the merit produced therein corresponds to the number of precepts received.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of protection provided by this:
first, the ability to generate protection.
Second, protection through gathering and sustaining;
third, protection through guarding and maintaining;
fourth, protection through remedying transgressions.
Fifth, the mild protection;
sixth, the middling protection;
seventh, the superior protection.
Eighth is pure protection.

Before receiving [the precepts], one first reflects: "I now wish to receive the prohibitory precepts that distance me from evil. This is called the moment when right reception can arise; this is called "appropriation" (parigraha).

Having completed the reception of the precepts, one contemplates the abandonment of all evils; this is subsumed under the five faculties as a superior condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). At that time, one consistently and intermittently maintains the seeds of the roots. One reflects upon and guards the precepts exactly as they were received. If, due to associating with evil friends or because of the afflictions (*kleśa*), a sense of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) arises, one immediately feels shame and self-reproach, thereby avoiding any breach or transgression. One ensures there is no failure that would lead to falling into the evil realms; this is called "guarding and maintaining" (*ārakṣā*).

If one is prone to forgetting and committing various evils, one should quickly give rise to mindfulness, confess and repent of these transgressions, and with shame and remorse reform oneself so as not to commit them again; this is called the characteristic of remedying transgressions.

Furthermore, if one upholds even a small portion of the wholesome path for only a short time, guarding it solely for oneself without encouraging others; if one does not speak well of it nor offer praise; and if, seeing others engaged in wholesome conduct, one neither rejoices in it nor feels delight—this is called the inferior [level].

Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts for the most part but does not do so until the end of one's life; if one maintains the precepts oneself and encourages others to do so, yet uses skillful speech without engaging in praise; and if, upon seeing fellow practitioners of virtue, one does not give rise to affection or delight—this is concealment therein.
Furthermore, if one fully upholds the prohibitive precepts and does not commit even the slightest transgression, this is called "superior.

Because one relies on these pure prohibitive precepts and is free from resentment, one permanently severs the root of breaking the precepts as far as the first dhyāna; because of reliance on śamatha, this concentration provides protection.
As it is in the first dhyāna, so it is in the second, third, and even the fourth.

Furthermore, there is another distinction: this is the profound abandonment through the path of meditative concentration, which is subsumed by the antidote that distances one from the root of breaking the precepts; this is the first purity of upholding the precepts.

Relying on this pure precept and protected by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one attains the vision of the True Truth and realizes the fruit of *anāgāmin*. At that time, all roots of violating the precepts are forever severed. If, relying on the preparatory stage of dhyāna (*anāgamya-dhyāna*), one attains the first fruit, at that time the roots for rebirth in the evil realms are entirely severed. Furthermore, there is the precept which is completely pure and cherished by the noble ones; by means of this second pure restraint of the prohibitions, it is called the protection of untainted (*anāsrava*) observance of the precepts.

This untainted precept (*anāsrava-śīla*) attains purification through its counteractive function at the time of becoming an Arhat; it differs from the fruit that results from the destruction of afflictions.
These eight kinds of precepts are combined into one, which is further divided into three:
first, the undertaking, practice, and protection [of the precepts].
Second is the protection of dhāraṇī;
third is the protection of purity.
The first three types of precepts constitute the protection of undertaking and practice.
Next, there are two kinds of protection through dhāraṇī: the practices of skillful means consist of the inferior, middling, and superior precepts;
the precepts of meditative concentration and the untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla) are called pure protection.
These three forms of protection increase in excellence in successive order.
For what reason did the Tathāgata teach these three types of precepts—namely, the bhikṣu-precepts, the upāsaka-precepts, and the eight precepts? It is due to three causes and conditions.
Among those beings to be converted, those who are able to abandon unwholesome conduct and further abandon sensual desire—regarding them, the Buddha speaks of the bhikṣu precepts;
among those to be converted, those who only abandon unwholesome conduct but do not abandon sensual desire—regarding them, the Buddha speaks of the upāsaka precepts.

Why is this? Because those living at home are confined in a place where afflictions arise and are constantly bound by fetters; it is difficult for them to fully receive and maintain the categories of precepts.
There are those being transformed who cannot abandon evil conduct and greed; therefore, the Tathāgata has taught the Eight Precepts for their sake.

Why is this? Because these individuals being transformed lack the capacity for both [the preceding precepts], they serve as the causal conditions for the first two precepts; they reflect within themselves that they are unable to endure the heavy prohibitions.

The first three parts manifest the abstention from unwholesome conduct; the subsequent four parts manifest the abstention from sensual desire; and the one part concerning celibacy manifests the abstention from both.
The meaning of the bhikṣu precepts is subsumed under four divisions:
first, the division of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*); [the other three follow].
Second, the precepts of restraint received in accordance with the full ordination;
third, the precepts for protecting the minds of others;
fourth, the precepts of complete observance.

Regarding the section on receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*): through the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), just as when receiving the great precepts, from the very beginning one relies upon these prohibitions of a bhikṣu; this is called the bhikṣu’s attainment of the section of full ordination.

From this point forward, in accordance with the bhikṣu precepts within the Prātimokṣa—namely, right livelihood and so forth—one constantly maintains and protects them in all circumstances; this is called being bound by the disciplinary rules in accordance with the full ordination.
Possessing these two aspects and being fully endowed with dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) is called the precept of protecting the minds of others.
The details regarding this conduct and sphere of activity are as described in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*, which will be explained later.

To perceive fear even in minor transgressions and refrain from committing them as if they were grave precepts, and to fully disclose any violations that may have occurred—this is called being complete in the observance of the precepts.

Based on the five powers, one gives rise to the four factors: through the power of faith, the precept of liberation is fulfilled; based on the power of diligence, the factor of right livelihood is perfected; based on the power of mindfulness, the sense faculties are guarded; based on the power of wisdom, the factor of dependent origination is fulfilled; and based on the power of concentration, the four factors are fully realized.
Why is this? If the five powers do not exist, then the four divisions do not exist.
Three of these divisions comprise the Upāsaka precepts.
What are these three?
First, that which is highly esteemed by others and free from the element of destruction;
second, the purification through repentance and reform when transgressions or faults have occurred.
Third, upholding [the precepts] without violation:
not taking the lives of others, not stealing the property of others, and not engaging in sexual misconduct—this is called the first part;
abstaining from false speech is the second part.
Abstaining from intoxicants is the third limb.
Furthermore, the eight precepts are comprised of five limbs. What are these five?
First, to refrain from harming others;
second, to refrain from harming both oneself and others;
third, to repent and reform when a transgression occurs.
Fourth, one maintains mindfulness so as not to lose the precepts;
fifth, one maintains mindfulness so that the factors [of the path] are not scattered.
To be free from taking life and free from stealing is called the first factor.
Abstaining from sexual desire is the second factor.

Why is this? By abstaining from sexual desire, one does not harm one's own person because of one's own wife and concubines; and by refraining from sexual intimacy with others, one does not harm the persons of others.
Abstaining from false speech is called the third part.
Next, abstaining from the three bases is the fourth part. Why is this so?

One should gradually train in and become familiar with [refraining from] singing, dancing, adorning the body with flowers and perfumes, using high or wide beds and seats, and eating at improper times; thus observing that the body is empty and selfless, one should maintain mindfulness of these precepts and not transgress them.
Abstaining from intoxicants is the fifth limb. Why is this?
Because one constantly reflects, "I now possess the precepts," and by relying on this limb, drunkenness, madness, and negligence can never arise.
The bhikṣuṇī precepts, the śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, and śrāmaṇerī precepts all belong to the category of monastic precepts; therefore, these precepts are obtained by relying upon the bhikṣu precepts.
The Upāsikā precepts belong to those living at home; because the precepts are similar, they are no different from the prohibitory precepts of an Upāsaka.
For what reason did the Buddha establish these two divisions—the precepts for Bhikṣus and the precepts for Śrāmaṇeras?
The bhikṣuṇī precepts are further explained as being threefold, namely: the bhikṣuṇī precepts, the śikṣamāṇā precepts, and the śrāmaṇerī precepts.
Because women possess many afflictions, they should receive these precepts in successive order; for this reason, the Buddha established the bhikṣuṇī precepts as a threefold set.
If a śrāmaṇerikā abides in the minor precepts, she may subsequently receive the śikṣamāṇā precepts in due order;

if she is able to abide in the śikṣamāṇā precepts, her categories of precepts increase, and she must not be granted full ordination immediately, but must certainly train in and practice the six rules for two years;
if she delights in abiding in this, then the full precepts shall be conferred.
In this way, after gradually observing minor precepts for a long time, one becomes able to observe the full set of precepts as time progresses.
For what reason is the handling of gold and jewels prohibited within the śrāmaṇera precepts, yet not forbidden in the eight precepts?

Because this śrāmaṇera abides in the precepts of renunciation, these two categories—namely, the pleasures of the five desires and the amusement of adorning the body—are utterly incompatible with one who has left the household life.

Regarding the two types of heedless indulgence, the former category is addressed by citing past examples to prohibit them; thus, three kinds are said to be abandoned: namely, singing, dancing, and music; adorning the body with perfumes and flowers; and high or wide couches. Furthermore, eating at improper times prohibits the second category.

Regarding the prohibition against handling gold and silver: since this gold and silver serves as the foundation for all worldly possessions and is considered the most excellent among all things, why are the two precepts concerning singing, dancing, and adorning the body—separated in the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras—combined into one within the eight precepts?
Because these are incompatible with those who have left the household life, they are strictly regulated as two;
because they are not incompatible with those who remain in the household life, they are made one as a minor offense.
Should one commit an infraction, there is only a single confession required.
If a renunciant violates these two precepts, they must perform two types of repentance.
For what reason are eunuchs and those who are impotent not permitted to leave the household life and receive full ordination?
If these eunuchs and others were to become bhikṣus, they would be capable of committing the offenses of women;
if they were to become bhikṣuṇīs, because they can engage in physical contact, they would be capable of committing the offenses of men.
Since these two states are unfit for them to abide in, they are not permitted to leave the household life and receive full ordination.

Because these eunuchs and those who are impotent possess much affliction and are hindered by afflictions, they are unable to give rise to the power of right reflection; lacking this power upon which to rely for repeated contemplation and diligent cultivation of the pure holy life, how much less could they attain the supramundane noble Dharma?
Therefore, they cannot leave the household life to receive the precepts.
Why is this? It is difficult to find virtuous persons born in such a place who can be properly distinguished.

For what reason do eunuchs and those who are impotent receive the three refuges and the five precepts, yet are not designated as upāsakas or upāsikās? One is designated an upāsaka or upāsikā by virtue of associating with bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
These eunuchs and others, though they may well restrain their sense faculties, should not be constantly associated with bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs.

Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs must not associate with them in private or secluded places, nor engage in activities such as massaging; they are not permitted to associate with bhikṣus in the manner of upāsakas. Therefore, they cannot be designated as upāsakas.
If these eunuchs and others maintain the precepts well, they shall obtain merit equal to that of others.
What is neither precept nor non-precept?

Apart from the precepts and non-precepts previously described, whatever wholesome or unwholesome karma one performs through body, speech, or mind—all such cases may be understood as being neither precept nor non-precept. Regarding these two kinds of precepts—those received spontaneously and those received from another—the merits arising from them differ.
When not receiving the precepts, if one’s intention is the same, then the protection and maintenance [of the precepts] are likewise the same, and the merit produced is no different.
By how many causes and conditions does one fail to fully possess the prohibitions of a bhikṣu?
Briefly stated, there are six reasons for failing to obtain what one desires:
first, because the mind is corrupted;
second, because the physical faculties are incomplete.
Third, those whose faculties are incomplete;
fourth, those who have severed their roots of goodness;
fifth, those who are bound to others.
Sixth is for the sake of protecting the minds of others.
If a king has imprisoned someone out of fear of bandits or calamities, or if one is burdened with another's wealth and fears being unable to survive, they might think:
"I am now suffering and find it difficult to stay alive; these are the kinds of miseries I endure because I live as a householder."

"All those who have left the household life live in peace and security; therefore, I shall now leave home to join the assembly, so that it will not be difficult for me to find a livelihood while practicing the Way.
Thinking thus, he immediately left the household life and, out of fear, undertook the observance of the precepts.
In some places, there is a disciplinary rule: "Do not let the bhikṣus know that I have committed a transgression, lest the Saṃgha, being in harmony, expel me from the assembly.
Because his mind is thus corrupted, he is not a bhikṣu who fully possesses the prohibitive precepts; this is called "corruption by way of the mind."
He further reflected:
"It is difficult to live as a householder.

If I were to renounce the world, it would be easy to provide for my physical needs and not difficult to seek my livelihood; furthermore, throughout the remainder of my life, I would be able to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) no differently than others who practice it."
Reflecting thus, he immediately went forth into homelessness.
Such going forth does not involve a corrupted mind; yet, although he has received the full precepts, they are not pure.

If he suffers from diseases such as goiters, leprosy, scabies, insanity, or consumption—as explained in the rules regarding prohibitions—this is called the second case of being deficient in the faculty of the body.
If one who has impaired their body were to obtain ordination, they would be unable to show respect to and make offerings to their teachers and elders.

Being thus unable to make offerings to others, yet receiving from them the pure alms of faith—clothing, food, bedding, and requisites provided by spiritual friends and teachers—one would find it difficult to digest such heavy gifts. Furthermore, one would be unable to increase wholesome dharmas; all previously cultivated virtues would be lost. For this reason, one with an incomplete physical faculty may not go forth or receive full ordination.

If one is a eunuch or a person incapable of male sexual function, because their sexual organ is impaired, they may not go forth and receive full ordination, according to the various causes and conditions previously explained.
There are three types of impotence:
first, total incapacity; second, occasional incapacity;
and third, untimely incapacity.
Third is the "maimed or damaged" [incapable person].
From birth, they have never possessed a male organ; this is called the person who is incapable despite being fully endowed.
Furthermore, there is the "half-month capable" person, meaning that during the first fourteen days they are incapable, and only on the fifteenth day are they capable.
Furthermore, one is able [to achieve arousal] when another person touches them, but unable when there is no touch;
likewise, one is able when seeing another engage in sexual desire, but unable when not seeing it—this is called "timely" and "untimely."

Furthermore, those who are wounded by swords or staves, afflicted by disease, fall [from a height], encounter poison or fire, or are cut off by incantations—such that they first possessed male organs but later lost them and became impotent—are said to be "maimed and impaired."
Regarding those who are impotent: first, there are those who were originally eunuchs (huanmen) and are thus impotent;
second, there are those who were not originally eunuchs but have become impotent;
third, there are those who were originally eunuchs but are no longer impotent.
If one touches his body and it can produce pleasure, this is called being deficient in the male organ (*puruṣendriya*).

As for those who have severed their roots of goodness (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*): having committed various heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), defiled a *bhikṣuṇī*, caused schisms among the internal or external paths, lived as a thief-monk (*caura-vāsa*), or engaged in various forms of non-cohabitation or lack of residence—because they have destroyed their roots of goodness, they are unable to receive the full precepts of restraint (*upasaṃpad-śīla*).

Why is this? Because such a person has no shame before themselves or others, is defiled by impurity, and lacks a sense of moral dread (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*), their wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*) diminish.

Regarding those who are "dependent upon others": this refers to those who are royal servants, those who conspire with the royal family, those known to the king, those who are about to pay off debts or interest to another, as well as the slaves of others, the laborers of others, those burdened by another's debt, those who have pledged themselves as collateral for a loan, and those whose parents do not permit it. Because they are dependent upon others, they are not permitted to go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Regarding "protecting the minds of others," this refers to those who have manifested as humans; because they protect the minds of others, they are not permitted to receive the precepts. Why is this?
It is because there are dragons who manifest themselves in human form to seek ordination, desiring to hear the True Dharma and seeking to receive full ordination.
If he had received full ordination, he would revert to his dragon body while sleeping due to the pressure of slumber.

Although he was already a bhikṣu, he would say, "I am a bhikṣu. When the āraṇyakas and upāsakas came to pay their respects and inquire after him, they would see his dragon body and would all harbor doubts regarding the bhikṣus, thinking: "These bhikṣus are not truly human beings; who would dare to make offerings to dragons and ghosts?"
One does not receive full ordination for the sake of protecting the minds of others.
Due to these six causes and conditions, one cannot leave the household life and receive full ordination.

Furthermore, if one is separated from the various teachers and the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), if the precepts are incomplete, if the number of monks in the assembly is insufficient, or if the boundary (*sīmā*) is not pure, one likewise shall not obtain the precepts.
Due to how many causes and conditions can one not receive the Upāsaka precepts?
Briefly stated, there are two:
first, because the mind is corrupted; [the second is because the body is impaired].
Secondly, because their physical faculties are incomplete,
those whose minds are impaired can never receive any of the prohibitive precepts.
As for those who are impotent, they may receive the five precepts, yet they cannot be called upāsakas, according to the various causes and conditions previously explained.
Furthermore, regarding the eight precepts, they cannot be received if the mind is corrupted, because one follows another or for the sake of gain and offerings.

If the mind is not pure yet one verbally declares the reception of the precepts—just as previously mentioned, there are various causes and conditions through which one cannot receive the precepts—then by being free from these conditions, one obtains the three types of precepts.
Furthermore, by how many causes is the bhikṣu precept lost?
First, by relinquishing the precepts;
second, by committing a grave offense.
Third, the loss of the faculties and the arising of both [sexual] organs;
fourth, the severance of the roots of goodness;
fifth, the end of life.
If one has already properly received the precepts of a bhikṣu, they are lost through five conditions.
When the Buddha-dharma is completely extinguished, those who have not yet received the precepts cannot receive them if they wish to do so, while those who have already received them do not lose them.

Why is this? Because at such a time, the final age has already arrived; there is not a single person whose mind is not corrupted who seeks to receive the precepts, let alone one who can attain the four fruits of the Path.
The *upāsaka* precepts [are lost] due to the arising of remorse, the extinction of roots of goodness, the exhaustion of one's lifespan, or the disappearance of the Buddha-dharma.
As it is with the bhikṣu precepts, so it is with the five precepts as well.

Furthermore, regarding the eight precepts: if one reaches the dawn of the following morning, or if the mind becomes corrupted, or if one’s life ends on that very day, then the eight precepts are lost.
What is the state of non-ideation?

Having abandoned desire for the Realm of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*), but not yet having abandoned desire for the higher realms, one engages in mental reflection, regarding this as liberation; it consists merely in the cessation of the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*). Such tranquility is called the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
This is a conventional designation; there is no separate entity.
Briefly stated, there are three types:
inferior, middling, and superior cultivation.

Because their cultivation was inferior, they fall back in the present life and are unable to swiftly resume practice to be reborn in the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva-deva). Their bodily radiance is narrow and inferior compared to that of other devas, and their lifespan is incomplete as they undergo regression midway.

Regarding those who practice the middling degree: if they fall away from their attainment, they will quickly regain it through renewed cultivation and be reborn in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*). Their radiance becomes increasingly superior, yet even before their lifespan has ended, they may again experience a middling regression.

As for those who cultivate the higher [stages], because they diligently practice and train, they do not fall away; if they are born there, they will be fully endowed with radiance and lifespan, and shall not die prematurely.

Why is this so? Because the attainment of birth brings about the cessation of the mind, and the mental enumerations (*saṃkhyā*) also cease; this is called "birth in the realm of non-perception" (*asaṃjñisattva*).
What is it that ceases?

Having abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), but not yet having abandoned desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), he applies mental reflection to seek a state of tranquility that is without sensation (*vedanā*) and without perception (*saṃjñā*). Seeing the defects within sensation and perception, he gives rise to weary detachment from the four dhyānas—the essence of sensation—and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*)—the essence of perception. Becoming weary of and detached from all eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna-samādhi*), he brings the mind and its mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) to complete cessation, thereby entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
It is called the "attainment of cessation" because it ceases the six consciousnesses, not because it ceases the *ālayavijñāna*.

This, too, is a provisional designation and not a substantially existent phenomenon; it likewise has three grades—inferior, middling, and superior—and its cultivation is as previously described, with the sole exception that "arising" is not mentioned.

Because those in training (śaikṣa) who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation—namely, the non-returners (anāgāmin) known as "bodily witnesses" (kāyasākṣin)—as well as those beyond training (aśaikṣa), can enter this absorption.
Both types of liberation (ubhayatobhāga-vimukti) do not cultivate the absorption of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), whether they be those in training or those beyond training.

Why is this? Because the noble ones do not perceive liberation in the places where they are born; the noble ones know and see that they will not be reborn in such places, as there are no superior realms apart from these. Being born in such places, one can never cultivate wholesome dharmas; it is a place of obstacles and difficulties.
What is space? Space is manifested solely as the absence of the realm of form.
For what reason is it called the "space-realm"?
The absence of all form is designated as "space.
Therefore, space is spoken of as a conventional designation and is not a real dharma.
What is cessation through non-cultivation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha)?

Because the conditions for their own manifestation are present, all phenomena arise; apart from these causes of arising, no other phenomena arise. This ultimate quiescence is called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), at which time all phenomena cannot arise.
When this life has passed, one is not born again; as for the future which has not yet arisen, it cannot be said to exist.
If a future dharma is destined to arise through causes and conditions, it will arise once they are assembled; by whom could it be obstructed so that it does not arise?
It is termed "permanent.
Therefore, there is no separate dharma called "non-analytical cessation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

When these practitioners of the training have already seen the Truths, their future births as egg-born, moisture-born, those born in Uttarakuru, or those born in the Heaven of Non-conception, as well as being female, neuter, impotent, rootless, or possessing dual sexual organs—along with the cessation of craving and aspiration such that they will not be born again—is termed non-analytical cessation; it possesses the same characteristic.
Why is this? It is impossible for these practitioners who have studied further to give rise to craving and attachment that could produce the karma for rebirth;
yet, because they have not yet uprooted the seeds of existence, their past karma causes them to take birth.

Why is this? These various factors dissociated from form and mind—from the characteristic of arising up to non-analytical cessation—are not mental concomitants within the category of mental phenomena; nor, within the category of form, are they visible or invisible.
For this reason, it is called non-associated form (*viprayukta-rūpa*).

Furthermore, that which is termed the discrimination of form and the discrimination of sound—whether it be disagreeable, or the locus of equanimity—consists of causes pertaining to sentient beings and causes not pertaining to sentient beings, as well as causes of both sentient and non-sentient beings.
Discrimination of objects refers to that which is produced by speech.
Discrimination of abiding is as previously explained.
Discrimination of fragrance refers to roots, stalks, bark, heartwood, leaves, flowers, and fruits; these constitute the discrimination of fragrance.
Within odors, aromas, and tangibles, there is no conceptualization of objective entities.
As for abiding in conceptualization, it is as previously explained regarding form.
Conceptualization of the characteristics of taste refers to [the distinctions of] sweet, bitter, and so forth.
Abiding is also as previously described.
Contact is of many kinds, as analyzed before.
As for the third object, it can be known throughout the ten directions.
The fourth object consists of the discrimination of the three periods of time.
The fifth object consists of the discrimination regarding the apprehension of the real and the unreal.
The sixth object is that which attains full apprehension within a single location.
In this way, one clearly discerns the various material objects within one's own sphere.
What is mental reflection?
It is that which is capable of generating consciousness.
Regarding those who are common and whose faculties are unimpaired, they give rise to consciousness together with clearly manifest objects.
To contemplate in this manner so as to produce the various consciousnesses is called "contemplation of the objective sphere of the aggregate of form."
Regarding mixed contemplation: when one enters and dwells within the aggregates (*skandha*) of the desire realm, the matter (*rūpa*) of the form realm arises within this very body.
How is it that the various matters of the higher realms dwell either in a separate location or not in a separate location from those of the lower realm?
The answer is:
They do not abide in separate locations, just like sand and water.
This is called the contemplation on the mixed portions of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); it is the completion of the contemplation on the analysis of the aggregate of form.

Chapter on the Mind-Ground, Part Three:

As stated in the Sūtra, there are six kinds of superior knowledge, namely: the aggregates (skandha), the sense bases (āyatana), the elements (dhātu), the four noble truths, dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), and the twenty-two faculties (indriya).
How is such supreme knowledge analyzed?
The *udāna* states:
Characteristics, meaning, and analysis; Succession, inclusion, and basis.
By relying on these six kinds of dharmas, one thoroughly understands the aggregates, bases, and so forth.
What is the characteristic of form?
It refers to eleven kinds: the eye and so forth, as well as the forms within the base of tangibles and the base of mental objects.
There are those that depend on the four great elements, and there are those that are the four great elements themselves; all of these possess the characteristic of resistance.
What is the characteristic of sensation?
It is said to be of six kinds, produced by contact with the eye and the other sense organs.
Furthermore, the three types of sensation have two kinds of bases, namely matter and mind. Bodily sensation depends on matter.
Why is this? Because the five sense organs are material.
If the faculties possess form and are experienced based upon the eye and so forth, these are called "bodily experience" (kāyikavedanā).
Why are the five faculties not themselves called the "body"?
The answer is:
Because the sense faculties have their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and because their functions are each distinct.
If they were of different characteristics, they would not share the same bodily characteristic; therefore, the sensation of the faculties is not called "bodily sensation" (*kāyikī vedanā*).
The answer is:
Because the sense faculties such as the eye exist without being separate from the body, and because feeling arises in dependence upon these faculties, it is called "bodily feeling" (*kāyikī vedanā*).
This explanation is without fault.

If you claim that there is no fault in the term "not separate," then since the mind is not separate from the body, mental feeling (*caitasikī vedanā*) would also be called bodily feeling; thus, all feelings whatsoever would be termed bodily feelings.
Answer: The body and the various faculties cannot be separated from one another, but the mind is not like this.

For instance, there are sentient beings born in the formless realm who possess a mind apart from a body; therefore, that which is received by the faculties is called "bodily sensation," while that which the mind receives apart from the body is called "mental sensation."
All these feelings have two names; that is to say, all feelings arise from three kinds of causal conditions:
first, the predominant power of the object;
second, the predominant power of mental attention.
Third is the excellence of sovereign power.
What are its characteristics?
They are of six kinds, as previously described.

Furthermore, there are six kinds of perceptions regarding the existence of birth: the perception of signs, the perception of signlessness, the perception of smallness, the perception of greatness, the perception of the immeasurable, and the perception of non-existence.
All these perceptions are divided into two types:
the first is mundane; [the second is supramundane].
Second, regarding the supramundane:
that which takes the desire realm as its object is called "small perception";
that which takes the form realm as its object is called "great perception."
Taking the sphere of infinite consciousness as its object is called the perception of the immeasurable.
Taking the sphere of nothingness as its object is the perception of the non-existent.
These, such as the desire realm and so forth, are called perceptions with signs.
The perception of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the perception of signlessness.
It is a supramundane perception, pertaining to those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those who have completed their training (*aśaikṣa*).
It is the characteristic of the perception that discriminates all signs.
What are the modes of activity?
As previously stated, there are six kinds; furthermore, there are five kinds of matters:
first, providing various objects for the senses;...
Second, because they are obtained together;
third, the distancing from the conditioned;
fourth, the arising of afflictions and karma.
Fifth is the attainment of mastery over the mind.
Briefly stated, there are three types:
wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
All that draws forth a fruit is called the characteristic of formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
What is the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*)?
It also has six kinds, namely, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.
Furthermore, this objective aspect (nimittabhāga) of consciousness is of three kinds:
first, the functional aspect;
second, the aspect of having multiple objects as its sphere.
Third, there are the various distinct divisions.

There are three divisions of function, six divisions of object, and three divisions of station; these various divisions, when analyzed, constitute eighteen modes of grasping objects as signs, which are the characteristics of the five aggregates.
What is the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*)?
As for "form" (*rūpa*), all forms—past, future, and present, even those near or far—are collectively termed "aggregates.
Likewise, from such forms up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), this total inclusion of all conditioned combinations is what is called the meaning of "aggregate."
For what reason did the Buddha teach the meaning of the "aggregates" (skandhas)?
It is because these aggregates are merely a collection and lack a real self; therefore, the Buddha taught that this is the meaning of the term "aggregate."
What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)?
It is analyzed into six types:
first, that which conforms to its kind;...
Second, following characteristics;
third, reliance on or non-reliance upon consciousness;
fourth, being apart from or not apart from consciousness.
Fifth is the sphere of perception;
sixth is the Akaniṣṭha realm.
All these forms—namely, the four great elements and that which depends upon the four great elements—are called "conformity to type."
There are three kinds of material forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*): first, pure matter;
second, pure objects.
Third is the common characteristic of the mental objects (*citta-rajas*). That which is common to all is characterized by substantial resistance; all forms (*rūpa*) are common characteristics.
Which of these are the supports for consciousness, and which are not?
That which belongs to the category of sentient beings is called "dependence.
Furthermore, there is the sphere of form where consciousness first enters and even until the arising of sensation; this is called "the dependence of consciousness.
To be apart from such form is called "non-dependence."
What is meant by "separated from consciousness" and "not separated from consciousness"?
Form that is not separated [from consciousness] is called "self-portion" (*svabhāga*), because it is commonly perceived and shared by all consciousnesses.

Furthermore, that which is separated from consciousness is called "non-self-portion" (*asvabhāga*); however, that which is similar, continuous, and capable of producing contact is termed "self-portion."
Although there is a similar continuity, because contact does not arise, it is called "not its own part.
There are three kinds of perception (saṃjñā) termed the objects of form (rūpa-viṣaya): first, the perception of form; [the second, the perception of sound; and the third, the perception of odor].
Second is the perception of obstruction;
third is the perception of variety.
The perception of form has three characteristics:
First, manifest form;
second, obstructive form;
third, aggregated form.
Because these three types of characteristics correspond to their respective objects, perceiving blue, black, and so forth is termed the "perception of form" (rūpa-saṃjñā);
that which obstructs one's movement is termed the "perception of resistance" (pratigha-saṃjñā);
and perceiving the characteristics of men, women, fields, houses, and so forth is termed the "perception of diversity" (nānātva-saṃjñā).
Regarding the "dusty forms" and the "Akaniṣṭha" (Ultimate Form), briefly stated, there are two aspects:
falling into the lower realms, and the predominant conditions of karma from the desire realm and the form realm.

As for the four spheres of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.), if one relies on the performance of action, there is no form; however, by relying on sovereign meditative concentration (*vaśitā-samādhi*), there is the form of sublime radiance.
For what reason does one attain mastery over all kinds of forms?
Because one cultivates the concentration of manifestation, these are the forms of sublime concentration.
What is the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha)?
There are five types of discrimination:
first, the category of sensation;
second, specific characteristics.
Third is the place of birth;
fourth is conceptualization and discrimination;
fifth is the place of cessation.
What is the category of sensation?
It is the dharma of its functional application.
What is its specific characteristic?
There are suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. Regarding pleasant feeling:
its arising is pleasant, its abiding is pleasant, and its cessation is painful; it is the causal condition for craving and attachment. Regarding painful feeling:
its arising is painful, its abiding is painful, and its cessation is pleasant; it is the causal condition for the departure from craving.
That which is neither painful nor pleasant is suffering because of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); thus, it is liberated from craving as its condition.
All these sensations are entirely suffering; this is called the common characteristic of sensation (*vedanā-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
What is the place of birth?
From sixteen types of contact (*sparśa*), the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) arises.

What are these sixteen? They are: contact of the six sense faculties; obstructive contact; contact based on verbal expression; painful contact; pleasant contact; neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact; contact of desire; contact of aversion; contact of ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*); contact of knowledge (*vidyā-sparśa*); and contact that is neither knowledge nor ignorance (*naivavidyā-nāvidyā-sparśa*).
Taking objects by means of the faculties is called contact of the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-sparśa*).
Thinking by means of objects gives rise to obstructive contact (*pratigha-sparśa*).
Producing speech by means of the mind is called contact dependent on speech (*adhivacana-sparśa*).

There are three kinds of contact regarding sensation: those based on bondage and those based on liberation. Contact with desire, hatred, and delusion is based on bondage; contact with clarity, non-clarity, and ignorance is based on liberation.
What is conceptualization and discrimination?
All Buddhas have eight kinds of discrimination:
how many kinds of sensation are there?
What is the arising of feeling?
What is the cessation of feeling?
What is the path leading to the cessation of feeling?
What is the practice for the cessation of feeling?
What is the gratification of feeling?
What is the danger of feeling?
What is the cessation of feeling?

There are three kinds of feelings distinguished by their characteristic of arising; because there is the accumulation of contact, there is the accumulation of feeling, as explained at length in the Sūtra.
These are the eight aspects that distinguish the aggregate of feeling:
First, discrimination of specific characteristics;
second, discrimination of manifest causes;
third, discrimination of the cessation of causes.
Fourth is the discrimination between the present and the future;
fifth is the discrimination regarding the path to the cessation of sensation;
sixth is the discrimination regarding the application of turbidity.
Seventh is the discrimination of purity;
eighth is the discrimination of the locus where sensation ceases.
These are called discriminations.

What are the bases for the cessation of sensations? In the first dhyāna, the faculty of grief ceases; in the second dhyāna, the faculty of suffering ceases; in the third dhyāna, the faculty of joy ceases; in the fourth dhyāna, the faculty of pleasure ceases; and in the attainment of cessation, the faculty of equanimity ceases. This is called the analysis of the bases for the cessation of sensation.
What is the aggregate of perception?
It is divided into five types:
first, that which conforms to categories;
Second, following characteristics;
third, inversion;
fourth, non-inversion.
Fifth is determination (*niścaya*).
That which grasps the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an object and gives rise to the cognition of a phenomenon is called "conformity to type" (*anuvyañjana*).
There are six types of conformity to characteristics, as already explained previously.
Although the objects apprehended differ, they all involve the perception of common characteristics and are thus termed "conformity-characteristics" (anulakṣaṇa).

Ordinary beings, lacking wisdom and with their minds shrouded by ignorance, give rise to false conceptualization; relying on two and a half views, they produce the four inversions. Relying upon what is impermanent, they claim it to be permanent—this is the cultivation of the notion of permanence.
Based on the view of existence (satkāyadṛṣṭi), two inversions arise: namely, conceiving suffering as pleasure and the impure as pure.
Based on the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the inversion of a self arises; that is, grasping at the characteristic of a "self" within phenomena where there is no self.
Furthermore, there is what is called "perversion of mind" for householders, which corresponds to what is called "perversion of view" for renunciants.
Additionally, there is "perversion of perception," which refers to the arising of false conceptions regarding the four types [of nutriment]; this is termed perversion of perception.
To give rise to conceptualizations of faith based on a determinative cognition regarding these four types of categories is called the perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
What is non-perversion of perception (*saṃjñā*)?

When wise persons, being free from ignorance (*avidyā*), give rise to correct reflection (*samyak-manasikāra*), they perceive impermanence in the object that is impermanent, suffering in what is suffering, impurity in the object that is impure, and non-self in the object that is non-self; to give rise to such perceptions of correct cultivation is called non-perversion of perception.
To be able to give rise to faith and joy regarding these four kinds is called non-perversion of mind.
To possess right view and right knowledge regarding these four kinds is called non-perversion of vision; this is called non-perversion of perception.
What is certainty?
There are five types of discernment:
first, certainty regarding the object;
Second, the determination of function;
third, the determination of conventional designation;
fourth, the determination of unreality.
Fifth is the determination of the actual object (*vastu-niścaya*).
Grasping the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an object or grasping its similar appearance constitutes the determination of the object.
The arising of sensation (*vedanā*) toward that object and grasping its distinct features is called the determination of function (*kāritra-niścaya*).

Based on oneself and others, the characteristics of names, birth, lineage, and so forth, which constitute the objects of conceptualization according to conventional discourse, are called the determination of designations.
Apprehending objects through inversion is called "unreal determination.
Apprehending objects as they truly are is called "determination of the real meaning.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?
There are five kinds of discrimination:
first, that which refers to objects;
second, distinct abiding.
Third is impurity;
