fourth is purity;
fifth is the object.
The six types of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) that, through their superior power, draw forth results are called the "object of formations" (*saṃskāra-viṣaya*).
The accumulation and aggregation of dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), such as birth, aging, and duration, is termed "distinctive abiding formations" (*pṛthag-vihāra-saṃskāra*).
Why is this? Because they are each distinct, they are called "distinct abodes and practices.
The practice of the three poisons and so forth is termed "impure."
The wholesome roots such as faith and so forth are called "pure conduct" (*śuddhacaryā*).
As with the five preceding types, that which is known together with objects and so forth is called "phenomena" (*vastu*).
What is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*)?
Discrimination is also fivefold:
first, the sense bases;
second, impurity.
Third, by way of reliance;
fourth, by way of abiding;
fifth, by way of multiplicity.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), consciousness relies upon external forms as its bases; these are called the sense-bases (*āyatana*).
In the pure heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), consciousness relies upon its own aggregates (*skandha*);

this constitutes name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Regarding the sense-bases of consciousness, there are two such bases. In the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), consciousness relies upon its own four aggregates and is designated as sense-bases. This is the classification of the sense-bases.

This consciousness of ordinary beings arises in impurity based on two kinds of pleasure: it is impure because it relies on the pleasure of utilizing present sensory objects, and it is impure because it relies on the pleasure associated with future sufferings such as birth and old age; thus, it is called "impure."

There are six kinds of bases for consciousness; these are the bases from which consciousness arises. Because the consciousnesses of the six sense-bases, such as the eye and so forth, arise based upon them, they receive the name "six.
It is, for example, like fire depending on chaff; fire from cow dung and so forth is likewise so called because it depends upon those [bases]. Thus it is named "basis" (*āśraya*).
The analysis of the four stations of consciousness is as explained in the Sūtras.
The aggregates, based upon their respective objects, serve as the stations for the mind.
Regarding the station of consciousness within the realm of form, it is explained in detail as in the Sūtra.
"Furthermore, I say that consciousness does not go to the east, nor to any other direction.

Within this present life, one who does not delight in nirvāṇa, but attains for oneself tranquility, coolness, and mastery over the Brahma-realm—I say such a person is as described in the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata."
The four stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*) will be explained in detail later.
Furthermore, there is a brief explanation of the three stations of existence with conditions (*sopādāna-vihāra*) and the station of ultimate peace with conditions (*upādāna-vihāra-śānti*).
By teaching these three, the Buddha reveals the four stations of consciousness.
The categories of afflictive objects upon which afflictions depend and abide are called "afflictive attachment.
These two types are termed "objects of attachment":
the first being the object itself;
The second is grasping (*upādāna*).
Regarding the object: when afflictions take craving as their condition, they declare, "This is my possession," which is precisely grasping at the object.
Through the affliction of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), one conceptualizes, "This is I."
Furthermore, there are four kinds of bodily fetters, such as craving; these are the causal conditions for karma and constitute the grasping of objects.
As previously stated, that which is clung to is the dwelling place of the mind.
Why is this? Because the objects of all afflictions depend upon the mind to abide.
Just as dust easily settles on a damp garment, or as seeds flourish in fertile soil,

so too do ordinary persons who have not yet attained wearying detachment— whose consciousness is led by the feeling that serves as the antidote to craving— attain rebirth in future lives with all its components fully complete.
Until one has abandoned the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), that which causes this rebirth to be fully realized is called "abiding.
This continuous succession of births is called "birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra*).
The remainder is as previously explained regarding the conditions for abiding.
Thus, all these are called the abodes with objective conditions (*sālambana*).

Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), various consciousnesses come and go; within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is said that the mind sinks and arises. In these three places, one abides until the end of one's lifespan.
Just as in the two aforementioned locations, there is birth, growth, and maturation, so too by this measure, one knows the ultimate extent of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
If anyone were to speak otherwise than this meaning, it would merely be a difference in phrasing; in principle, there is no distinction.
Why is this? Because the meanings of words are distinct and without conceptual differentiation.
If there were someone who asked [such questions], one would be unable to answer and would instead reflect:
"How shall I respond?
If he should give an answer, he later reflects further:
"I am truly foolish; not knowing the solution myself, I have answered the question of another."

Therefore, when a wise person temporarily suppresses all fetters, such as craving for everything from the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of formations, they are unable to produce karmic fetters; because they possess wisdom, these are fundamentally and eternally exhausted.
How is this known?
Householders rely on the fetters of greed and hatred; thus they produce karma through the conditions of attachment to worldly pleasures and the conditions of fear and aversion.

For renunciants, the fetter of clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) gives rise to karma: the affliction of clinging to precepts shares the same characteristic as greed, as they aspire to be reborn in the heavens; the affliction of clinging to [false] views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) shares the same characteristic as hatred, as they revile *nirvāṇa*.
These fetters arise from conceptualization based upon the ground of the mind.
Because these afflictions are extinguished through their antidotes, that which seeks to grasp desire, form, and so forth as objects is forever extinguished.
Because these are extinguished, the various consciousnesses no longer abide in the four stations where they were previously deluded, for the counteractive consciousnesses are truly pure.
Thus one comes to know that the stations are tranquil.

Because conditions have ceased, that which was destined to arise in future lives will be fully exhausted; its continuity having been attained, it shall not arise again. This is called "abiding with conditions.
The profound purity of the tranquil *amala-vijñāna*, which serves as the antidote to worldly consciousness, is termed "non-abiding."

Furthermore, this consciousness does not arise through conditions; because it has well-cultivated the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*), it cannot produce karma; because it has well-cultivated the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*), it is able to be content; and because it has well-cultivated the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*), it abides in immovability.

As with the four meanings mentioned previously, one attains right liberation; through contemplative practice, one does not grasp at or become attached to sensory objects, to a self, or to what belongs to a self. Consequently, all sensory objects such as form are extinguished and disintegrate, and the mind is free from craving.

When the mind is thus utterly purified of these various marks, because consciousness is pure, it does not undergo self-destruction, nor is it extinguished by other conditions, as there is no continuity.
Not entering further birth in the ten directions, and because there is no craving for life or death, it is said that there is no seeking or desire.
The mind is like a tree; feeling is like its shadow.
At that time, both are absent; therefore, there is no tree, and therefore there is no shadow.
Because the worldly mind has ceased, it is said that what appears is now extinguished; this is the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*).

Because one trains in liberation, one first attains tranquility as explained in the sequence; because one is liberated as one beyond training (aśaikṣa), one attains purity; and because the four remaining [defilements] are extinguished, one attains mastery over the Brahma realm.
Question:
Why is it not said that consciousness is a station of consciousness? Answer:
It is said that consciousness is not obtained as impure because of its own characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). Why?
Because the Tathāgata has taught that the mind is pure by its own characteristic.
The four bases (*āyatana*) are not like this, because all afflictions (*kleśa*) are extremely impure.

One knows that desire and so forth are subtle and difficult to perceive; the form-aggregate (*rūpa*) and others are not like this, as they are not the causes of affliction in the same way that the form-aggregate and others are.

There is no sentient being who gives rise to craving and attachment toward a single station of consciousness as they do toward form and so forth; therefore, the Buddha taught that consciousness is not a place of abiding. This is called the analysis of the stations of the aggregate of consciousness.
Regarding the various types of discrimination, there are three explanations:

first, the mind with desire and the mind without desire, the mind with anger and the mind without anger, as explained at length in the sūtras, up to the states of not yet having attained liberation and having attained perfect liberation; what the Tathāgata has taught in this regard is called the first.
This is because it is free from conceptual differentiation regarding the differentiation of realms. Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are four types of mind:
wholesome, unwholesome, afflicted, and non-afflicted.
Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are three types of mind, with the unwholesome excluded.
The formless [realms] are likewise.
There are two types of untainted [phenomena]:
namely, those of the learner (śaikṣa) and those of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
The wholesome mind of the desire realm is divided into two types:
that acquired at birth and that acquired through training.
There are four non-defiled [minds]:
They are: fruition, deportment, craftsmanship, and transformation.
In the desire realm, the single type of transformation is acquired at birth, such as that of devas, nāgas, and ghosts, which does not result from the fruit of cultivated wisdom.
Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is no craftsmanship;
within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is only the result of maturation (*vipāka*).
A wholesome mind is like ascending a high mountain; this is called the second classification according to the realms.
Furthermore, there are distinct mental states due to the various kinds of afflictions and conceptualizations.
Within the desire realm, there are five [types], which are destroyed by the paths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the path of cultivation.
The five types in the form and formless realms are likewise; thus, there are fifteen in total.
Furthermore, there are sixteen [aspects] of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*).
This is called the third [category], the analysis based on cessation (*nirodha-vibhāga*).
The first is detachment (*vairāgya*); furthermore, the three grades of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) are analyzed as the three samādhis.
First, those who cause movement; second, those who do not cause movement.
First, those who do not attain concentration; second, those who attain concentration.
First, those who are not pure; second, those who are pure.
In the first category, there are those with defiled minds whose minds are obstructed by desire and so forth;
furthermore, at certain times, there are those with wholesome minds or neutral minds for whom desire and so forth do not arise.
In this way, one discriminates between minds with desire and minds without desire.

In the second stage, or at other times, when relying on internal meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and settling the mind on a single point, because the mindfulness of objects has ceased, the mind becomes distracted by the five sense-objects; because it sinks excessively, it is obscured by sloth and torpor (*kausīdya*).

To eliminate laziness, because the mind is not properly settled upon the object of joy and bliss, it becomes momentarily agitated; however, by correctly apprehending the object, the mind does not become agitated.
Sinking and agitation constitute an afflictive hindrance to the mind’s tranquility; when sinking and the like are extinguished, the mind immediately attains tranquility.
Through right reflection, one attains the fundamental dhyānas; this is called mental concentration (*citta-samādhi*).
To depart from the characteristics of these prior concentrations is the unconcentrated mind.
Because one reaches the ultimate path, there is right cultivation; because one reaches the ultimate cessation, there is right liberation.
Apart from the two preceding characteristics, there is improper cultivation and improper liberation.
Grasping the various marks of meditative concentration to identify the third category is called the discrimination of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
What is meant by the explanation of the aggregates (skandhas)?
There are eight kinds of aggregates in sequence:
the first is the aggregate of birth-activity (janmakarma).
Second, the path of cultivation;
third, that which is produced by the causes of defilement;
fourth, that which is produced by abiding.
Fifth, performing with discrimination;
sixth, performing according to the location;
seventh, performing according to the degree of coarseness.
The eighth is the "action like a vessel.
What is "action by birth"?
Visual consciousness arises depending on the faculty and depending on the object; it is likewise for the mental consciousness depending on the mind and depending on the object.

According to the *Anupūrvika-sūtra*, it is first stated that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is the basis for mental factors (*caitasika*), and subsequently it is stated that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) and mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) reside therein; this is called the sequence of production (*utpatti-krama*).
What is the sequence of the path of cultivation?
To eliminate the four inversions, the four foundations of mindfulness are taught.
Regarding form, which is impure yet erroneously conceived as pure, the foundation of mindfulness of the body is taught.
Regarding feelings, one calculates them as pleasant; this is called the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Based on perceptions and formations, one falsely calculates a self where there is no self; this is called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Based on the mind, which is impermanent, one erroneously calculates it as permanent; this is called the application of mindfulness to the mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*).
What is the sequence of the causal process of defilement?
A man perceives the form of a woman and gives rise to passionate attachment.
For what reason does he experience it?
Because of craving for the taste [of sensation].

One who craves the taste of sensation relies on the perversion of perception; the perversion of perception relies on the afflictions of mental formations; and the afflictions of mental formations rely upon the aggregate of consciousness and upon the sense faculties and their objects.
The arising of experience through the engagement with sense objects (*viṣaya*) and the grasping of various kinds of objects is called perception (*saṃjñā*).
The arising of various afflictions (*kleśa*) through the engagement with present objects is called formations (*saṃskāra*).

Based on these afflictions, impure consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises; because it gives rise to suffering such as birth in future states through wholesome and unwholesome karma, one further obtains impurity. Thus, consciousness is explained last.
What is the sequence of abiding and functioning?
Consciousness abides in four bases:
first, form;...
Second is feeling;
third is perception;
fourth is mental formations.
Why is this? Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), form (*rūpa*) is the abode of form, because form is fully present within the desire realm.
Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is said to be the abode of feeling (*vedanā*).
Why is this? Because feeling is what manifests.
Regarding the three formless realms, it is said that they are the abodes of perception.
Why is this? Because it manifests through perception (*saṃjñā*).
Regarding the fourth emptiness, it is said to be the place where one dwells and practices.

Why is this? Because great volition manifests; because eighty thousand great kalpas are the fruit of that volition; and because it is said that abiding in the four stations is called the sequence of abiding in action. As for the sequence of analytical action:

by means of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), one sees forms and hears sounds, thereby knowing others; by means of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the mind possesses highs and lows, giving rise to suffering and pleasure; by means of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), one knows names, clans, and lineages; by means of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one discriminates between the foolish and the wise; and by means of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), one conceives of a self within the aggregates.
This is called the sequence of differentiation.

As for the sequence of occurrence, for example, in the case of householders, conflict arises due to the causes and conditions of form and feeling; in the case of renunciants, conflict likewise arises due to the causes and conditions of perception and mental formations; in both cases, consciousness serves as the common cause and condition.
Regarding the sequence based on coarseness: form (*rūpa*) is the coarsest, as it is the object of the six consciousnesses.

Next, the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is explained, because there are three types of feeling; because its characteristics, such as male and female, are easily discernible; because greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth are easily recognized within it; and because it is difficult to discern apart from feeling when considering perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Regarding the sequence of their functions, such as those of a vessel and so forth: form is like a vessel, because it contains the three types of sensation;
sensation is like food and drink, because it benefits or harms the body;
and perception is like a condiment, because it grasps the specific qualities of sensation.
The formations are like the food that arrives because they bring about suffering and pleasure;
consciousness is like the eater because it employs sensation and the other [mental factors].
What is it that appropriates?

How many aggregates (*skandha*), how many bases (*āyatana*), how many elements (*dhātu*), how many causal factors (*pratyaya-bhāga*), how many instances of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), and how many faculties (*indriya*) are included?

From the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*): the aggregate of form is one aggregate; it comprises ten bases and ten elements; it is described as a partial portion of the base of mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*) and the element of mental objects (*dharma-dhātu*); it comprises a partial portion of six conditions; it is also described as a partial portion regarding what is possible and what is impossible; and as for the faculties, there are seven.

Regarding that which is subsumed under the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*): one part of the aggregate of phenomena (*dharma-skandha*), one part of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), one part of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), one part of the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), three parts of the conditions (*pratyaya*), and five among the bases of power (*indriya*).

Regarding the inclusion within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): it comprises a small portion of one aggregate, one dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*); it comprises a small portion of the three conditions (*pratyaya*) and the categories of the possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*). It does not, however, include the faculties (*indriya*).

Regarding that which is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): it is also said to include a portion of one aggregate, the sphere of mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*), and the realm of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*); a portion of four conditions (*pratyaya*); a portion of five conditions; the section on the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*); six [factors] among the faculties (*indriya*); and a portion of three faculties.

Regarding that which is subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha): it comprises one aggregate, one base (āyatana), and seven elements (dhātu); two factors of dependent origination; a portion of the conditions; the factors of the possible and the impossible (sthānāsthāna); and among the faculties (indriya), it is said to consist of one faculty and a portion of three faculties.
In this manner, from the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) up to the faculties (*indriya*), they mutually encompass one another.
Furthermore, there is another type of inclusion: the ten aggregates and other such phenomena encompass their own seeds; this is called "inclusion by difference" (*anyathā-saṃgraha*).
The inclusion of the aggregates (*skandha*) and other phenomena within their own and common characteristics is called "inclusion by characteristic" (*lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*).
The fact that the aggregates and other phenomena pervade all locations is called "inclusion by birth" (*utpattisaṃgraha*).
The fact that the aggregates and other phenomena abide in feelings such as pleasure is called "inclusion by distinct abiding" (*pratyekasthānasaṃgraha*).
When the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth arise simultaneously, it is called "inclusion by non-separation" (*avinirbhāga-saṃgraha*).
When the phenomena of the aggregates and so forth exist within the three periods of time, it is called "inclusion by time" (*kāla-saṃgraha*).
When the phenomena of the aggregates and so forth arise in dependence upon a location, it is called "inclusion by location" (*sthāna-saṃgraha*).
Because the dharmas such as the aggregates (skandhas) are equal in five ways and so forth, it is called "complete inclusion" (paripūrṇa-saṃgraha).
Because the dharmas such as the aggregates are not complete in their individual parts, it is called "partial inclusion" (pradeśa-saṃgraha).
Because the dharmas such as the aggregates are the suchness (tathatā) of their marks, this is called "true inclusion" (bhūta-saṃgraha).
As with the aggregates (*skandha*), there are sixteen groupings (*saṃgraha*) up to their conjunction with the sense bases (*āyatana*).
Furthermore, there are three types that encompass all phenomena (*dharma*): the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and the sense base of mind (*manāyatana*).
What are these aggregates?
Based on how many kinds of forms does the aggregate of form arise?
Based on how many bases is the aggregate subsumed under name produced?
The aggregate of form arises based on the six bases.
First, the place of dependence;
second, the place of residence;
third, the place of bedding and furniture.
Fourth, the locus of the faculties;
fifth, the locus of the basis of the faculties;
sixth, the locus of the various stages of meditative concentration (dhyāna-bhūmi) according to their functional capacity.
Consciousness relies upon seven bases to encompass the arising of the aggregates:
first, desire;
second, form; [and so forth].
Third is dust;
fourth is sensation;
fifth is examination.
Sixth is the skillful means of pure conduct;
seventh is purity.
These four points—beginning with desire—are taught for those who live as householders.
The object of observation is the diligent observance of the precepts by one who has gone forth;
the skillful means of pure conduct leads to the attainment of future-dhyāna;
and seventh, through purity, one attains the fundamental dhyānas.
For the sake of four types of persons, the seven [bases] are explained as four.
The analysis of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) will be explained in detail later; it is based on the analysis of form.
The summary (uddāna) is as follows:
Regarding substances and atoms, arising forms and continuities,
karma and so forth, moments, and the solitary [senses], as well as the objects of the senses— these are said to be ten. Furthermore,
how many substances are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and subsumed within the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*)?

If the eye-consciousness has a single substance as its basis, then because it is a pure form that is not separate from the category of [material] inclusion, there would be seven substances: namely, the eye, the body, earth, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
Because they are subsumed within the three realms, it is said that there are ten entities: the seven kinds as previously described, plus water, fire, and wind.
Just as with the entity of the eye, so it is for the ear, nose, and tongue.
Excluding the four faculties, the body faculty consists of nine substances.
Why is this? Because, being devoid of the four [sensory] faculties, the body faculty can arise independently.

Furthermore, there is the sound-element (*śabda-dhātu*), which does not endure for long; therefore, it is spoken of separately as "there being a location where there is sound. Thus, there is a classification of eleven material objects (*rūpa-ādi-viṣaya*), such as visible forms and so forth.
Such qualities as smoothness and so forth, up to firmness, are all included within the sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
These are designated by specific names based on the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and smoothness is described in reliance upon the purity of the four great elements.

Based on solidity, heaviness arises; based on impurity and lack of solidity, coarseness and lightness arise; for the sake of purity, it does not combine with [solidity] and thus softness arises as contact. When earth and water mix, cold contact arises. When the sustaining causes are incomplete, hunger and thirst arise, and weakness also arises. When the sustaining causes are complete and the great elements are in a state of equilibrium, the power of that balance gives rise to the contact of satiety. When the great elements are unsuitable and food and drink are difficult to digest, various contacts of illness arise. Based on the transformation of the body and the disharmony of the four great elements, the contact of aging arises. Based on the transformation of the life-faculty and the disharmony of the four great elements, the contact of death arises. Because of the inequality of the blood, afflictions arise; thus, from consuming poisonous or evil food and drink, there is the temporary contact of fainting. When earth and water intermingle, turbid contact arises. Through coming and going, moving and turning, and the arising of mental afflictions, the contact of fatigue arises. Apart from these aforementioned conditions, the contact of rest and movement arises.

When the four great elements are in harmony, the physical form does not diminish; there arises a sense of well-being that harmonizes with all tactile sensations. The separate abiding of the four great elements is said to be of six kinds: namely, the pure great elements together with the impure great elements, the solid together with the non-solid, the non-appropriated, and the mixed.
All objects, whether equal or unequal—such as visible forms up to tactile sensations—are known by two types of consciousness:
the individual sense-consciousness and the mental consciousness; they may be known simultaneously or not simultaneously.
Within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), although fragrance and taste do not manifest, it is not that their seeds are absent.

Because there is no solid food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) and because desire for food has been abandoned, the two objects—fragrance and taste—are not present; furthermore, because the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue have no active function, [the seeds] nonetheless exist as latent potentials.
When the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) comprises form, there are nine substances:
the four great elements (mahābhūta) and the five sense objects (viṣaya) that depend upon them.
All other forms are conventionally designated as aggregates.
Within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), there are two kinds of form (rūpa):
substantial existence (dravyasat) and conceptual existence (prajñaptisat).
Form perceived within meditative concentration through the mastery of that concentration is called substantial existence.

These—the transformations resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-nirmāṇa*), the objects of consciousness shared through concentration (*samādhi-sādhāraṇa-viṣaya*), and the matter of morality and non-morality (*śīlāśīla-rūpa*)—are all merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*).

Furthermore, they are the results of the sphere of matter as an object of concentration (*samādhi-viṣaya-rūpāyatana-phala*), because they correspond to the sphere of matter within concentration (*samādhi-sthāna-rūpa-saṃprayukta*).

Based on the great concentration (samādhi), worldly dharmas arise; based on both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) concentrations, form (rūpa) is a worldly dharma and not a supramundane dharma. Why is this?

Because there is the causal condition of meditative concentration involving conceptualization (*saṃskāra-vitarka*), all those who possess concentration may be able to produce form or unable to produce form, just as in the case of transformation-birth (*nirmāṇa*).

If one does not engage in such conceptualization but relies on prior mastery, being free from obscuration, pure radiance will spontaneously arise and manifest in the present life; this is called "existence through conceptualization" (*vastu-saṃskāra*).

By the power of contemplating liberation, one perceives various forms; yet these forms, while not yet manifest before one, exist as mere designations and are not the objective dust of supramundane meditative concentration.
The forms of supramundane concentration cannot be contemplated as the forms of the desire or form realms.
What is meant by "form distinct from the form realm"?
It is because it is supremely vast and pure, emitting radiance;
it is supremely subtle and refined, being beyond the sensory objects of inferior faculties.
There is no sensation of suffering, because it transcends all suffering;
it cannot be conceptualized, for it abides within the subtle particles of atoms (paramāṇu) without obstruction;
and it manifests as coarse or subtle according to the mind’s perception.
These are the five kinds of distinctions.
Briefly stated, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) possesses six characteristics:

its own characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), its common characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), the characteristic of the relationship between the support and that which is supported, the characteristic of function (vṛttilakṣaṇa), the characteristic of activity (karmalakṣaṇa), and the sublime characteristic (praṇītalakṣaṇa).

The specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the four great elements—earth, water, and so forth—are solidity, moisture, heat, and motion; the purity of the various faculties, such as the eye, is their specific characteristic. These are called specific characteristics.
That they all possess resistance (*sapratigha*) is the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of form.
The four great elements are the basis; that which depends upon them are the five sense objects, which constitute the characteristic of mutual relation.
Because the internal bases possessing form exercise predominance, various external objects are able to arise.

There is a mass of form that receives the name "solid contact" (*khara-spraṣṭavya*); there is moisture, heat, motion, and mixture, which function as internal bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*). This is called the characteristic of function (*kāritra-lakṣaṇa*).
The four great elements, such as earth and so forth, which provide support, cohesion, maturation, and growth, constitute the characteristic of activity (*karma-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, there are other karmic activities which shall be explained in detail later.
Subtle matter consisting of atoms is called "exquisite characteristic" (*sūkṣma-nimitta*).
There are three kinds of exquisite characteristics:
There are three kinds of subtle [atoms]: the subtle through analysis (*vibhāga-sūkṣma*), the subtle through birth (*utpatti-sūkṣma*), and the subtle through mastery (*vaśitva-sūkṣma*).
Because it is the limit of analysis, the *paramāṇu* is the subtle through analysis.

Because it is the limit of the arising of atoms, such as wind and so forth, up to the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the form within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the form within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are called "subtle" due to their mastery over subtlety; thus they receive the name *paramāṇu*.

As the Buddha’s sutras state: "Abiding in the midst of human life, one attains a mind of equanimity; one cultivates one's own mind, adorns one's own mind, and makes one's mind sovereign. Dwelling together in one place, they do not obstruct one another, nor do they cause any affliction or harm."

If, after this, one is born as a Great Brahmā Sovereign in Akaniṣṭha, and for the sake of hearing the Dharma descends to Jambudvīpa below, he divides a single hair-tip into sixteen parts; if the earth occupies only one such part, all the devas may dwell together therein without mutual obstruction—this is called the "atom of mastery" (vaśitva-paramāṇu).

Thus, when contemplating the categories of material phenomena within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), how many types of distinctions are there regarding the characteristics of atoms (*paramāṇu*)?
Briefly stated, there are five; these shall be explained in detail later.

Because they are analyzed by the fundamental wisdom of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, because they are distinguished by their categories, because they are individual parts, because they are shared companions, because they lack spatial dimensions, because the ultimate wisdom of the analysis of matter determines them to be atomic divisions rather than corporeal measures, and because atoms are neither produced nor destroyed, it follows that a mass of matter is not produced from atoms.

When analyzing atoms (*paramāṇu*), there are fifteen types: the five faculties beginning with the eye, the five objects beginning with form, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the form of phenomena (*dharmarūpa*).
The analysis of their individual characteristics is called the "distinctive portion" (*pratyeka-bhāga*); the combination of these atoms is the "associated portion" (*sahāya-bhāga*).
Why is this? Because the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of earth and the other elements are not separated from one another.
For what reason do they possess the property of resistance (*sapratigha*)?
Because they do not depart from a single location and dwell together with their companions, there is no lack of unobstructedness.
This is like the union of the mind and the great elements, as their faculties are similar.

The arising of various functional activities constitutes their similar karma; because they serve as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the various forms harmonize, and by collectively functioning as the faculty, they are able to arise.
If it were not thus, there would be no such thing as a combination.
The eye-consciousness and its objects, as well as the sense organs and their objects, would be useless; therefore, these companions cannot be separated from one another.

There is a category of form that is either obstructive or non-obstructive, such as the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) up to the form of the Brahma-world; this is called the "associated portion" (*sahabhū-bhāga*).
Because it is the ultimate limit of form (*rūpa*), atoms of form possess no spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*).
Because they do not aggregate, the atoms of form that do aggregate possess spatial dimensions; apart from a single spatial location, there are no atoms of form.
Regarding the five kinds of atoms previously mentioned, there are five kinds of eyes:
the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the noble wisdom-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Buddha-like eye.
Of these five kinds of atoms, how many are the objects of each eye?
The fleshly eye and the divine eye cannot see it; the other three eyes can see it.

Why is this? Because only when matter is aggregated can the divine eye perceive its internal and external, upper and lower, front and back, as well as light and darkness. It does not see atoms (*paramāṇu*), because they are distinguished by cognition, and because the characteristics of atomic matter do not constitute a separate substantial entity.
Why can it be known and stated that atoms (paramāṇu) are neither produced nor extinguished?
Answer:

Because they arise through the complete conjunction [of conditions] obtained previously; and because they have not yet attained a distinct individual substance when the subsequent moment has not arrived, they are extinguished therein.

For example, by means of five characteristics of water droplets, one understands through the contemplation of atoms (*paramāṇu*) that they do not truly exist as a combination of material forms; rather, atoms abide by virtue of their own intrinsic nature—this is the first [characteristic].
The arising and ceasing of atoms through improper mental attention is the second.
The abiding of atomic matter, whether accompanied by associates or separated from them, is called the third.
The abiding of matter in conjunction solely within atoms is called the fourth.

The aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*) can produce other forms, and these produced forms are distinct from the atoms themselves. Likewise, when one contemplates atoms through improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), it is like a person with a distorted mind grasping at various signs; by abandoning the five kinds of improper reflection and contemplating atoms correctly, one attains the five kinds of merit.

Because the composite sense-fields consist of atoms (*paramāṇu*), one practices the path through their functioning; thus, regarding all objects of experience, there is no cause for doubt, and one acts with mastery—this is one merit.
The gradual increase and preeminence of the path that extinguishes the view of a self-body is the second merit.
The arising of the means for the extinction of the conceit "I am" is the third merit.
When various afflictions arise and, having arisen, are momentarily stilled so that the mind attains purity, this is the fourth merit.
By means of the two gates of liberation—emptiness and signlessness—one attains the wisdom of cultivation; these are the five merits.
Regarding "arising," briefly stated, there are five kinds of arising for material things:
arising by dependence, arising from seeds, arising through attraction, arising through growth, and arising through decay.
What is meant by "arising in dependence"? Derived matter arises in dependence upon the four great elements; therefore, the four great elements are not themselves called derived matter.

These four great elements are the voidness in which derived matter arises; this conjunction of matter is the basis of the four great elements. By knowing the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of matter, one understands that within this conjunction there exists matter and yet there is further voidness. Not perceiving a specific characteristic, one knows there is no separate matter. In brief, it is understood that while there are characteristics, they are not [inherently] existent characteristics.
If one speaks of existence when it is not perceived as empty, this can be understood through analogy.
If there is a common basis, do these obtain the same object or different objects?
There are two meanings: by way of measure (*pramāṇa*) and by way of power (*bala*).
If they were not of equal magnitude, one would have to obtain a small cognition;
since such a small cognition is not obtained, that position is untenable.

If it is argued that there is a distinct power because the objects upon which it relies differ, yet no such distinct power exists apart from their own characteristics, then the claim that this power differs is likewise untenable. This is called "arising in dependence."
What is birth from seeds?
It arises from its own seed.

For example, as with a grain of rice, through many causes and conditions, the elements such as sprouts, flesh, earth, and ash arise. Encountering various causes and conditions, hard things become soft and soft things become hard; that which is not hot becomes hot and that which is hot becomes not hot; that which is motionless becomes moving and that which is moving becomes motionless.

Thus, whether it be beautiful color or unattractive color, because they possess their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they arise from their own seeds in various ways; this is called "arising from seeds.
What, then, is "drawing forth" (*ākṣepa*)?
The internal sense bases arise through the increase of karma; they are produced without moving external objects.
For example, just as the receptacle world arises due to the牵引 (attraction/pull) of past karma, so too do the internal sense bases arise.
Just as one performs karma, so do the sense bases of the five destinies arise.
All external material objects are drawn forth by three kinds of karma:
first, as in Uttarakuru, where the environmental retribution arises spontaneously, extending from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven.
Second, external forms arise through the drawing power of one's own manifest karma, as in the case of the fifth heaven.
Third, external forms arise based on the karma of another's thought, as in the case of the sixth heaven.
This is called "drawing forth birth" (*ākarṣaṇotpāda*).
What is "growth birth" (*vivardhanotpāda*)?

It is birth obtained through the fulfillment of various causes and conditions; that is to say, as form grows and gradually becomes complete, or as sprouts and the like grow through irrigation by water and rain—this is called "growth birth."
That which arises apart from growth is called "destruction-arising" (bhaṅga-utpāda).

As for the arising of derived matter (bhautika-rūpa), it is like various substances ground together with a stone; because their distinct characteristics cannot be discerned individually, it is not like the accumulation of various items such as sesame, beans, or wheat in one place, where their different species can be known.

Why is this? It is just as the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) can produce functional activity, serving as the dominant cause (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) to arise.
If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise from their own seeds and bases, why is it said that derived matter arises in dependence upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Answer:
When the four great elements increase or decrease, the derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) that they compose likewise undergoes benefit or harm accordingly.
This is because, for example, visual consciousness does not arise separately apart from the four great elements.
For example, just as the great earth supports the four great elements, or as thread supports a garment, the great earth increases or decreases due to three causes and conditions;
through skillful means, it is able to cause the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) to increase or decrease.

Due to the causes of craftsmanship, the causes of karma, and the mastery of meditative concentration, the earth element is able to produce the three types of power regarding the increase and decrease of form.
What are these three?
There are three powers: the power of increasing, the power of serving as a receptacle, and the power of being a productive cause.

Because the water element possesses the power of moistening, the fire element the power of maturing, and the wind element the power of drying, these functional activities cause the increase or decrease of derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) through the increase or decrease of the four great elements (mahābhūta).

When the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise in a manner similar to prior karma, they attain similarity; therefore, derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) resembles the four great elements. This is called the causal condition of karma. Regarding mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi-vaśitā*):

having previously reached the great earth, one can later cause derived matter to increase or decrease. Just as one can transform the four great elements and derived matter—taking earth as water and taking water as earth—this is mastery over meditative concentration.

Furthermore, to speak briefly, there are five kinds of causes and conditions by which four factors of differing characteristics produce different effects: by the power of the four great elements, by the power of effort, by the power of incantations, by the power of supernormal faculties, and by the power of karmic actions.
From this point onward, until reaching the place of birth, the various forms aggregate within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
By what cause and by what condition does the seed-cause itself draw forth the karma that brings about rebirth?
This is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
For what reason does birth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) exist?
How can it be believed?
Furthermore, it is impossible for the mind and its mental factors, once they have ceased without support, to be reborn in another location because they cannot travel there.
If one were to consider this analogy to be like an echo, that interpretation would be incorrect.
It exists because the sense faculties are disordered, as in the case of seeing two moons.
If one were to argue that there is no intermediate state (antarābhava) by using the reflection in a mirror as an analogy, this too is incorrect, for the face is not diminished [by its reflection].
The analogy of a reflection is not so.
Furthermore, if you contemplate that the mind grasps an object without an intervening consciousness, your analogy is incorrect because the mind does not travel [to the new location].
If these analogies are intended to refute the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), this argument is invalid.
Therefore, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) truly exists and is credible; it is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Having already arisen through the volitional thought of the stage of rebirth, what is it that goes forward to take up a place of birth and arises in another realm of form?
Answer:
The four great elements (mahābhūta) precede [the derived matter] as they move toward the place of rebirth, because the four great elements serve as its support.
At that location, the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) arises simultaneously with the great elements; it arises because the four great elements obstruct the place of birth.
Furthermore, because derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is pervasive in its own characteristics and is not separate from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it is able to obstruct the place of arising.
It can be understood that the four great elements, such as earth and the others, possess both coarse and subtle aspects.

As explained in sequence: because the earth element supports, it performs an activity and can be said to have a result; the flowing, burning, and blowing of the water, fire, and wind elements are the activities of these three great elements.

All sounds are merely subject to arising and ceasing; they are produced through the conjunction of forms and do not persist for long. They are perceived within both the internal and external spheres; depending on their simultaneous production in various locations, they are heard everywhere as they pervade all places.
Just as when a flame reaches its destination, there is no before or after and no slowness or swiftness.
This wind is of two kinds: moving and non-moving.
That which forms a wheel is non-moving; that which travels through space is moving.

That which functions among objects is always compliantly sustained as an illusory transformation; that which sustains the illusory transformation is itself immovable—anything other than this is mobile.
As for the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*), whatever is comprised by light and darkness is all derived form (*bhautika-rūpa*); this is called the space element.
Because its distinct characteristics cannot be known apart from light, darkness, and so forth, the space-element is also immovable.
Where there is constant illumination or constant darkness among sentient beings, it is immovable therein;
if it were otherwise than this, it would be called "moving."
That which is comprised by the pure, luminous, and radiant clarity resulting from the aggregation of matter is "matter"; that which is not clear and luminous is likewise comprised by matter.
As for "shape," it refers to length, shortness, and so forth.
Is this a substantial dharma or a mere designation?
Answer:
This is a mere designation.
Why is this? Because it is a collection.
To say "this is a location" or "this is a shape" is merely a matter of verbal expression and mere measurement; within the eight characteristics, there is no distinct meaning [beyond these].
If one regards that which is visible as being visible, its essential nature is composite, just like a chariot and so forth;
because wisdom differs [in its mode of apprehension], it is said to be a provisional designation (*prajñapti*).
Furthermore, regarding the form derived from the fruit of meditative concentration within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), one perceives only that which possesses form.
Why is this? Because the causes for the arising of other odors, tastes, and tangibles are absent, and they no longer serve a function.
Thus, regarding the wind moving through space, there are no particles such as odors that arise simultaneously with it; rather, because they are in close proximity, the wind possesses fragrance.
Furthermore, regarding that which emerges from the wheel within the light: if the various great dharmas and objects such as fragrance were not present, they could no longer manifest.

The form that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-phala-rūpa*) arises within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) based upon meditative concentration; it does not arise from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Because it resembles the original color, it is also called "derived form" (*upādāya-rūpa*), yet it does not depend upon the four great elements.
Within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), how many kinds of phenomena are visible and possess resistance?
Answer:

One kind consists of two types: those that are the objective domain of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and are distinct from the form included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*); all remaining forms are invisible.
Furthermore, regarding those parts that possess obstruction, they constitute shape within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
As for the continuity of mental reflection, how many kinds of flows are there within the aggregate of form?
Answer:
There are three kinds:
first, the basis;
Second is that born of retribution;
third is that nurtured by growth.
As for the supports, there are four:
The basis of retribution, the basis of growth, the basis of inequality, and the basis of essential nature.
Regarding the basis of retribution, there are two types:
first, that of the preceding category; [and second, that of the subsequent category].
Second, the continuity of the preceding category, because it is drawn forth by retribution and so on.
That which arises subsequent to retribution is called "continuity.
There are two types of nurturing:
There is nourishment throughout the fullness and nourishment through the characteristics.
Regarding "fullness," there is growth of the material form; it grows in dependence upon food, drink, sleep, celibacy, and meditative concentration.

Furthermore, regarding mutual increase: because they depend on food and drink, depend on the state of fullness, and constantly experience pleasure, and because they ripen according to time, they attain growth.
All material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) attain growth by depending on these two kinds of conditions.
Regarding formless phenomena (*ārūpya-dharma*), they increase solely through the augmentation of their characteristics (*nimitta*).
The various forms (*rūpa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are nourished by the four nutriments (*āhāra*). What are these four?
Volition (*cetanā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), nutriment-lump (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), and contact (*sparśa*).
Because the former two kinds of nutriment have not yet drawn forth [the result], they are the causes for arising (*utpatti-hetu*).

The latter two kinds of nutriment are the causes for subsistence (*sthiti-hetu*); contact-nutriment is the condition for the subsistence of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and the others, while the remaining factors such as sleep are also able to cause growth.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), matter increases not by dependence on edible food, nor by dependence on sleep, nor by dependence on the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

All material sense-faculties follow these two streams; apart from these two kinds, there is no other stream upon which they depend. It is observed that the continuity of karmic fruition increases, matures, and becomes robust at certain times.
Why is it that what is comprised by retribution is not called "nourished" (*aupacayika*)?
Answer:
Because this matter of retribution remains as it is placed, abiding without increase or decrease.
Regarding the nourishment of the continuity: because the continuity of the conditioned environment (niśraya-vipāka) involves both opposition and compliance, it undergoes increase and decrease.
As for that which is not the matter of the sense faculties (indriya-rūpa), it all possesses three flows:
the mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) rely upon the flow of the basis (niśraya-srotas) and the flow of retribution (vipāka-srotas).
If there is increase based on the predominance of characteristics, then within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and form (*rūpa*), there is no retribution-born [matter].
All other phenomena are to be understood in the same manner as the mind and its mental concomitants (*citta-caitasika*).
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all internal and external forms arise as the result of karmic maturation (*vipākaja*).
Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), with the exception of odors and tastes, the remainder are results of maturation.
Furthermore, within the desire realm, the deficiency of sense faculties is also a result of maturation.

Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), all faculties that are complete are results of maturation (*vipāka*); the element of sound (*śabdadhātu*) therein is also a result of maturation. Because it is not [itself] sound, this is called the contemplation on the continuity of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
As for "action" (*karman*), it is subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and extends from the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) up to the element of wind (*vāyu-dhātu*).
All four great elements possess five kinds of action: the action of manifesting and transforming this earth element; [the action of supporting];
[the action of cohesion]; [the action of maturing]; and [the action of moving].
The activity of being the locus that supports;
the activity of acting as a basis;
and the activity of mutual opposition.
The function of the element of equality (samatā) is to increase karma.
The functions of the water element (abdhātu) are flowing, cohesion, moistening, resistance, and growth; these constitute its five kinds.
The functions of the fire element (tejodhātu) are illumination, maturation, destruction, resistance, and growth; these likewise constitute its five kinds.
Regarding the function of the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*): lightness, movement, causing contraction, expansion, and growth—these are called the functions of wind.
Furthermore, there are four primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that arise in the production of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), and each also possesses five functions.
What are the five?
First, that which can produce;
second, that which provides a basis.
Third, the dwelling place;
fourth, the superior maintenance;
fifth, the increase.
Why is this? Because it reaches [the state of] arising prior to the actual generation, it is called "that which can generate.
Because that which has already arisen does not depart from its locus, it is called "providing support."
Because they share a similar nature in terms of increasing, decaying, and so forth, they are called "abodes" (*sthāna*).
Because they can sustain [beings] without diminishing their measure, they are called "sustainers" (*dhṛti*).
Because they cause [beings] to increase, they are called "increasers" (*vivardhana*).
Why is it that the objects of the eyes and ears—namely, visible forms—possess both wholesome and unwholesome qualities, whereas other objects do not?
Answer:
Briefly stated, there are three reasons:
There are weak, medium, and superior volitions (*cetanā*).
What constitutes the weak?
It is the volition at the time of reflection, the volition at the time of determination, and the volition at the time of performing the action.

Because wholesome and unwholesome bodily and vocal actions arise based on the two types of form produced by the most superior volition (*cetanā*), the form of karma is either wholesome or unwholesome; therefore, other sensory objects (*viṣaya*) cannot be like this.
Is the movement and shifting of the combination of form (rūpa) a different characteristic or a non-different characteristic?
Answer: It is said to be a non-different characteristic.
Why is this? Regarding this object, whether it has already arisen or has not yet arisen, whether it has already perished or has not yet perished, the sense of "motion" is untenable.
If motion occurs after that which has already arisen has moved, it would lack its own intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If it has not yet arisen, there is no movement; if it has already perished, it cannot undergo movement, for it is identical to that which has not yet arisen.
If it has not perished, then there would be no distinct entity with a clearly defined characteristic of motion that reaches those causes and conditions; this argument is untenable.
Therefore, movement has no separate, substantial existence;
this is called the functional aspect of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
As for the momentariness [of thought], it is because this [aggregate] is complete [in each instant] and because the aggregate of form perishes moment by moment.
Why is this? Because when practicing the Dharma, one attains birth and cessation without obstruction.
At that time, the cause of birth is itself the cause of cessation; this interpretation is not correct.
Why is this? Because a different effect cannot arise from a single cause;
furthermore, once [the effect] has arisen and abides, the distinct characteristics of the cause do not manifest.
Therefore, the practice of the Dharma ceases of its own accord and does not depend upon the earth.
The cessation of mindfulness proceeds without obstruction, just as fire and other such things serve as causes for destruction.
If one were to contemplate it in this way, the meaning would not hold, because [the mind] arises and ceases simultaneously with fire and the like.
It is not as in the case of prior births, where only the cause can produce [the effect].
To claim that things such as fire are extinguished by an "extinguishing cause" is incorrect. Why is this so?
Because cessation does not coexist with conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
If cessation were already present, the continuity of all formations would have already been severed within that cessation; for this reason, they cannot coexist.
As for cessation (*nirodha*), it cannot function as a cause for cessation because its essence is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, this is not the case.

If cessation were the cause of cessation, they could not exist simultaneously; since there would be no difference between the preceding and succeeding moments of that which acts as the cause of cessation, all phenomena in a continuous stream (*saṃtāna*) would never arise.
If cessation were a distinct entity, then apart from the meaning of the cessation of a thing, a separate characteristic of cessation could not be found; therefore, this is not the case.

Furthermore, if one considers that fire and other factors act as concomitants of cessation to bring about destruction, then mental states, mental factors, lamps, flames, and so forth would possess an inherent cessation of their own nature and thus would not exist [as they do]; therefore, this is not the case.

Furthermore, if the powers were to mutually establish one another, then because both would be capable of cessation, there would be no distinction such that "this is the object of cessation" and "this is the agent of cessation. Therefore, this is not the case.

Furthermore, if two types of phenomena were each fully endowed with their respective capacities for mutual cessation, yet each possessed only half the capacity and lacked the other half, this would not be the case. Therefore, it is not so.

In this way, within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), these factors are equally divided because one contemplates their own nature as ceasing moment by moment, because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and other phenomena preclude the causes of cessation, and because they preclude two kinds of causes for cessation.
How is this known?
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have the mind as their fruit, it can be understood that they all possess momentariness (*kṣaṇika*).
As for "solitary" [matter]: is it distinct from the specific characteristics of derived matter produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), or is it not distinct?
Answer: There is a distinction. Why is this so?
Because it perceives distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Such distinct characteristics refer to different sense organs and objects;
this is because other sense organs and their primary elements (*mahābhūta*), as well as other derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), are either transcended or not transcended [by that perception].
The fragrance from various flowers does not transfer into the sesame seeds and so forth, because it does not transfer through transformation or non-transformation.

For instance, when substances such as ghee are boiled and mixed, their color, taste, and other qualities undergo transformation, whereas their solidity and other such characteristics do not; therefore, we know that there exists a distinct category of derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).
The four great elements and their derived matter possess distinct characteristics, yet their substance is one.
It is like seeing a tree trunk and giving rise to two cognitions; while the apprehension of their characteristics differs, their substance is one.
The first is because it is the object of doubtful cognition;
the second is because it is the object of decisive cognition.
This analogy is incorrect; for although they possess distinct characteristics yet function as a single entity, the same should apply to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
How do we know this?
These four great elements each have their own distinct characteristics; if these four great elements were definitively a single entity, there would not be four.
This argument is incorrect.
Therefore, derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are distinct entities; this is what is meant by the meaning of "exclusive" and "non-exclusive.
Regarding the contemplation of objects: among all phenomena, how many faculties (*indriya*) and how many sense-objects (*viṣaya*) are comprised within the category of matter?
Answer:
The five colors are the faculties (indriya), and the six colors are the objects (viṣaya).
As for what constitutes the faculties, it is that the various objects constitute the spheres of perception.
Regarding "those whose faculties are not impaired," the detailed explanation is as in the Sūtra.
Within the first stage (*bhūmi*), by how many kinds of causes and conditions are the various faculties impaired or not impaired?
The answer is that there are two kinds:
First, they are weak and inferior;
second, they have all been lost.
Were it not for these meanings, all would constitute faculties (*indriya*).
Briefly stated, there are four causes and conditions for transformation.
The first arises from external conditions.
How is this known?
Because external objects involve opposition and compliance, inflict harm upon others, and undergo the harm inflicted by others, they are called external conditions (*bāhya-pratyaya*).

Second, regarding internal conditions (*ādhyātma-pratyaya*): as with unwholesome reflection (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) occurring within, the faculties (*indriya*) such as desire that arise therefrom diminish; whereas through right reflection (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), samādhi, and so forth, the faculties increase.
Third, they arise through karmic conditions; because past karmic conditions have varying degrees of strength, there are those that are desirable and those that are undesirable.
Fourth, they arise from their own substance; because all the sense faculties rely on their own characteristics, they are sometimes impaired and sometimes benefited.
Furthermore, how many ways are there for the root of the mind to be destroyed? The answer is:
there are four.
The first is that which arises from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa).
Among the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), any one of them may shroud the mind; this is an act performed by a distracted mind.

An act performed by a distracted mind is like being possessed by a ghost or similar entity. Regarding "seeking what has not yet been attained": it refers to those who, while not yet having attained the four formless absorptions (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*) or the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñāḥ*), claim to have attained them because they have given rise to a perverted mind; thus, it is called "seeking what has not yet been attained."
When that which is to be accomplished has not yet been mastered—such as extensive learning or various crafts—the mind undergoes destruction based on these four meanings.
Furthermore, how is it that objects such as form are clearly perceived by the sense faculties?

Visible form does not reach the eye, yet it is clearly perceived by the eye; even when the object is not extremely subtle, it is seen with clarity. Furthermore, regarding visible forms that are unobstructed, located where there is light, and situated neither too far nor too near, such external objects are clearly perceived by the eye; indeed, there are sentient beings who perceive visible forms even within a dark room.
There is only one kind of invisible matter: as with the various objects previously mentioned that are not seen by the fleshly eye, all are seen by the divine eye.
As for sound, it does not reach [the ear] when there is no obstruction.
If there are those who arrive, whether in light or darkness, they do not exceed the subtle; when they abide at the location of the object, they attain clarity.

As for odors, tastes, and tangibles that reach their respective faculties and abide at the location of the object—those visible forms seen by the divine eyes of these beings—even if they are subtle, obstructed, or distant, once they abide at the location of the object, they are all clearly perceived; if they do not abide at the location of the object, they cannot be seen.
Furthermore, as for the noble ones who possess the noble eye of wisdom, they clearly perceive all kinds of forms and colors, just as the six types of objects were explained regarding the first bhūmi.
How is this to be interpreted?
The first object refers to all forms that enter into the world of sentient beings as well as the receptacle world.
Second, based on the three natures, there are all distinctions:
first, the distinction of characteristics; [and so forth].
Second is the discrimination of objects;
third is the discrimination of abiding.
Such discriminations as blue, red, white, and so forth are explained at length.

As for the discrimination of things (*vastu-vikalpa*), it consists of informative and non-informative form (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*), form that is discipline (*śīla-rūpa*), form that is non-discipline (*aśīla-rūpa*), and form that is neither discipline nor non-discipline (*naivasaṃvara-nāsaṃvara-rūpa*).

As for the discrimination of abiding (*sthiti-vikalpa*), it refers to forms that are agreeable, disagreeable, and those involving equanimity; this is called the discrimination of form (*rūpa-vikalpa*).
The discrimination of sound refers to causes consisting of sentient beings, causes not consisting of sentient beings, and causes consisting of both sentient and non-sentient beings.
The discrimination of phenomena refers to that which is produced by the mouth.
Regarding "abiding in discrimination," it is as previously explained.
Regarding "discrimination of fragrance," this refers to roots, stalks, bark, heartwood, leaves, flowers, and fruits; these are the discriminations of fragrance.
Within fragrance, taste, and touch, there is no discrimination of substantial entities.
Regarding abiding in conceptualization, it is as previously explained for form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the conceptualization of the characteristic of taste, this refers to sweet, bitter, and so forth;
abiding therein is also as previously described.
Contact is of many kinds, as distinguished previously.
The third object is that which can be known within the ten directions.
The fourth object is the distinction of the three periods of time.
The fifth [consciousness] can be known through the discrimination of grasping at the real and the unreal.
As for the sixth object, it attains full grasping within a single location.
In this way, it clearly discriminates its own respective material objects.
What is the contemplation that can produce consciousness?

When the various sense faculties are intact and not impaired, and the mind arises simultaneously with a clearly manifest object, such contemplation can produce the various consciousnesses; this is called the contemplation on the objective sphere of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Regarding "mixed contemplation": when one enters and dwells in this state within the aggregates of the desire realm, the matter of the form realm arises within this very body.
How is it that the various matters of the upper realms dwell together with those of the lower realm in a single location, rather than in separate locations?
The answer is:

They do not abide in separate locations, just like sand and water; this is called the "contemplation of the mixed portions" of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), not the "contemplation of the distinct portions" of the aggregate of form.
The Treatise on the Storehouse of Determination, Scroll II, Part B.
